subtopic: hiding an addiction from a sponsor
sentence: When he asks why I missed last Tuesday's meeting, I'll say I had a stomach bug. The bug is a closed loop — it has a beginning, a middle, and an end, and nobody will follow up on it in three weeks' time. The actual reason is that I was nursing a hangover and could not bear the idea of sitting in that room performing the version of myself I am supposed to be performing.

subtopic: lying to a friend about disliking their work
sentence: He published the article last weekend and I haven't read it. When he asks if I saw it, I'll say I did and that I particularly liked the way he opened it. Most articles have an opening, and most openings can survive a generic compliment without any specific detail being required. The compliment is doing nothing more than telling him I value the relationship enough to perform attention to his work, which is itself, I have decided, a kind of attention.

subtopic: concealing a near-miss accident from family
sentence: I nearly went off the road on the motorway this morning, a real heart-in-mouth moment, and I am still slightly shaking. When I get home my husband will ask how the drive was. I'll say fine, the usual. Telling him would make him anxious every time I drive for months, and the moment has passed and the car is undamaged. The shake in my hands I'll explain, if he notices, as too much coffee.

subtopic: feigning enthusiasm for a friend's plan
sentence: She's planned a surprise party for her partner and wants my help with every detail, and her excitement is genuine and lovely. I'll throw myself into it, voice-wise, saying how perfect it'll be, how he'll love it. Privately I think he will hate being surprised in a crowded room. But she has decided, and my honest read would only worry her, so I keep the read to myself and supply the enthusiasm she came for.

subtopic: lying about whereabouts or activities
sentence: I'll tell the kids I was at the garage getting the tyres looked at. I've kept the receipt from the actual visit two months ago in the glove compartment, slightly creased, and I'll wave it vaguely if anyone asks. Children don't read the dates on receipts. Neither does my wife, normally, although I'd rather it never get that far.

subtopic: exaggerating busyness to avoid a request
sentence: A friend is going to ask me to read and give notes on her long manuscript. Before she can, I'll mention how I've taken on too much and can't seem to find a clear hour. The clear hours exist. But finding the clear hour is exactly what she'd be asking for, so I'm pre-emptively declaring it gone, dressing a simple unwillingness up as a scheduling impossibility.

subtopic: deceiving a sibling about an inheritance
sentence: When my younger brother asks why I'm pushing to sell the cottage rather than rent it out, I'll say the upkeep has been higher than expected and the tenants we've spoken to weren't reliable. The truer reason is that I want my share in cash now, and renting it out would tie my hands for years. The story I'm telling is rational and economic. The motivation underneath is impatience, and impatience doesn't poll well at family meetings.

subtopic: pretending an opinion is your own
sentence: My friend told me last week why she thought the film was overrated, and her reasoning was sharp. Tonight, at a different gathering, I'll offer that exact reasoning as my own considered verdict. She isn't here. The people who are will think I have unusually incisive taste in cinema. The opinion is hers; the credit, in this room, will be mine, and the two rooms will never compare notes.

subtopic: concealing a tattoo or piercing from family
sentence: My father thinks tattoos are something that happens to other people's children. The one on my forearm is covered, whenever I see him, by a sleeve I time my whole wardrobe around. In summer this requires planning. But the planning is cheaper than the conversation, and so I have become, in his presence, a man who is inexplicably always slightly too warmly dressed, and he has never thought to ask why.

subtopic: lying about a pet's fate to a child
sentence: The dog ran off during the storm and hasn't come back, and I think the truth is bleak. When my son asks, I'll say a kind family found him and loved him so much they wanted to keep him, and that we agreed because he'd be so happy with them. It is a lie with a soft shape. It lets a seven-year-old believe his dog is curled by a fire somewhere rather than lost in the cold.

subtopic: lying about a pet's fate to a child
sentence: When my daughter asks if her old cat is in heaven, I'll say yes, and that she's young again there, and chasing the birds she could never catch in the garden. I do not know what I believe about heaven. But my daughter is grieving and she is six, and the picture of a young cat chasing birds is one she can hold in her hands. The honest uncertainty is mine to carry, not hers.

subtopic: faking a sick day
sentence: I'll cough a bit when I drop the kids at school. The other parents will tell their kids' teachers, and the news that I was visibly unwell at the gate will travel through the village in a way I can't engineer myself. By the time it gets back to my office, three different mothers will have independently said I looked rough, and the alibi will have a small chorus behind it.

subtopic: faking a sick day
sentence: When my coworker rings to check whether I'm okay, I'll answer in a slightly hoarser voice than usual and keep the call short. I'll mention I've been asleep most of the morning, which both explains the hoarseness and discourages further calling. I'll thank her for ringing in a tone that suggests I'd rather be sleeping. She'll get off the phone within a minute, satisfied, and the sympathy will diffuse through the team.

subtopic: running a secret online life
sentence: When my partner asks why I sometimes head into the spare room at ten in the evening, I'll say I've been doing a bit of writing. The writing is real and is on the laptop in that room. The writing is also being posted under a pseudonym to an audience my partner does not know exists, and the messages I exchange with that audience are the part of the evening I value most. The writing is true. The audience is the secret.

subtopic: exaggerating a minor injury for sympathy
sentence: My knee aches a bit after the run, the ordinary ache of an unfit person. But there's a social thing on Friday I'd rather skip, so I'll start describing the knee as something that's really playing up, that I'm being careful with, that might need looking at. By Friday the knee will be the reason I stay in, and the ache, which will have faded by then anyway, will have done its job.

subtopic: feigning enthusiasm for a friend's plan
sentence: My friend has decided we should all learn to sail and has found a course, and she's bursting with it. I get seasick looking at boats. But when she asked who was up for it, I said me, definitely, this is exactly the kind of thing we should be doing. The seasickness will reveal itself naturally, on the water, where it can be no one's fault, rather than now, in the kitchen, where it would have to be a refusal.

subtopic: pretending to remember someone you have forgotten
sentence: The barista said good to see you again and asked if I wanted the usual. I do not remember being a regular here and I do not know what my usual is. I'll smile and say you know what, surprise me, which turns my blankness into playfulness. Whatever she makes will, by definition, be acceptable, and the small fiction that I am a familiar face costs me only the price of one slightly unexpected coffee.

subtopic: concealing a poor decision from a business partner
sentence: I hired the new designer against my partner's instinct, and three weeks in it's clearly a mistake. When he asks how she's settling in, I'll say she's finding her feet, which buys time. I'm hoping she improves before he notices, or that I can move her onto a quieter project where the cost of my misjudgement is harder to see. Either way, I'd rather he never learn his instinct was right.

subtopic: concealing a job interview from a current employer
sentence: My manager asked me, in passing, whether I was happy here, and I said very, without hesitation. I have an interview next week. But a hesitation would have been a thread for her to pull, and the cheerful, immediate yes closed the topic completely. The lie cost me one short sentence and bought me an undisturbed run-up to the door.

subtopic: downplaying a career setback to in-laws
sentence: If her brother brings up the redundancy at the family lunch, I'll laugh it off and say the package was actually quite generous and gave me space to think about what I really wanted next. The package was minimum statutory. The space is anxiety. The thinking is doom-scrolling at three in the morning. But the sentence is well-shaped and her brother, who has no real interest in the answer, will move on to something else within a minute.

subtopic: hiding an online purchase from a partner
sentence: The art print I ordered for the study cost more than my wife would consider sane. When she sees it on the wall, I'll say I picked it up cheaply at a charity shop years ago and only just found a frame for it. The charity-shop story is the perfect cover because it explains both the existence of the print and its supposedly low cost in a single, modest, hard-to-disprove sentence.

subtopic: embellishing a CV
sentence: I'll move the gap year to before the master's instead of after, which makes it read like a thoughtful interlude rather than a stalled job hunt. The gap year is the same year regardless. The interpretive frame around it is what changes. Recruiters love thoughtful interludes. They are suspicious of post-degree gaps. Repositioning the same twelve months earlier in the timeline is the cheapest legitimate-seeming rewrite available to me.

subtopic: hiding an online purchase from a partner
sentence: I ordered the handbag on a payment plan so no single large amount appears on any statement my husband checks. The instalments are small enough to vanish into the noise of the month. When the bag itself appears, I'll say a friend was clearing out her wardrobe and passed it to me. The friend has a real wardrobe and really does clear it out, which is exactly the kind of true detail a smooth lie likes to stand on.

subtopic: claiming a gift was exactly what you wanted
sentence: My partner's parents gave us a piece of art for the new flat that clashes with everything. I'll be the one who says how thoughtful, it really suits the place. It does not suit the place. But they were nervous about choosing for our home, and my warm certainty settles that nerve, and a settled nerve is worth more to the relationship than the wall is worth to me.

subtopic: feigning a scheduling conflict to decline an invitation
sentence: My team is planning a weekend away and I do not want to give up a weekend. I'll mention that I think I've got family staying then, that the dates might clash, said with just enough uncertainty to seem honest. The uncertainty is the craft of it. A flat lie can be checked; a hedged one, I think it clashes, simply makes people pencil me out and move on.

subtopic: inventing a flattering reason for a gift
sentence: I'm giving my friend the concert tickets I can no longer use, but instead of admitting I double-booked, I'll say I bought them with her in mind because I know how much she loves the band. The generosity costs me nothing, since the tickets were going to waste. But she'll receive it as a deliberate kindness, and a deliberate kindness banks more goodwill than an honest offloading of a sunk cost.

subtopic: concealing a tattoo or piercing from family
sentence: I had the script inked along my collarbone, low enough that a normal shirt hides it. At my sister's wedding I'll wear the dress with the higher neckline, the one I told her I preferred anyway. She thinks the choice was about the dress. It was about the two inches of skin the other dress would have exposed, and the questions from relatives that those two inches would have launched across the reception.

subtopic: exaggerating a minor injury for sympathy
sentence: I bumped my head on a cupboard door. It barely hurt. But when my mother phones I'll mention it carefully, say I felt a bit dizzy afterwards, and that I'm keeping an eye on myself. The dizziness is invented. I just miss the particular quality of my mother's attention when she thinks I might be unwell, and a knock to the head is the cheapest way to summon it.

subtopic: inventing a flattering reason for a gift
sentence: The flowers I'm bringing my girlfriend tonight are really an apology for cancelling on her twice this month. When I hand them over I'll say I just wanted to brighten her week, no occasion. Naming the cancellations would make the bouquet a transaction. Calling it spontaneous makes it a gesture. The flowers are identical either way; only the story I attach to them decides what kind of evening we have.

subtopic: covering up a broken household item
sentence: I snapped a slat on the wooden blinds yanking them too hard, and I've adjusted them to a half-open angle that hides the gap. They've been at that angle for a fortnight now. My wife thinks I've developed a preference for the light that way. I have developed a preference, but it's a preference for her not noticing, which is a different thing dressed up as a decorating choice.

subtopic: manipulating a relationship through omission
sentence: I'll tell him my friends were busy this weekend. The truth is they invited me to a dinner I wanted to go to alone, because being around him in that particular group has been wearing me out lately. If he ever found out, he'd be hurt, so I've decided that hurt is something we both don't have to deal with as long as I keep the calendar slightly fuzzy in his head.

subtopic: lying about why you skipped a social event
sentence: I didn't show up to the networking evening because the whole format makes me want to walk into the sea. When my manager asks if I went, I'll say I got held up on a client call that ran long. Client calls are revered. They explain any absence and reflect well on the absentee. The format that actually defeated me will never be named, and I'll nod when she says it's a shame I missed it.

subtopic: feigning enthusiasm for a friend's plan
sentence: He's planned an elaborate weekend itinerary for my visit, hour by hour, and he showed it to me with such pride. Half of it is the kind of thing that exhausts me. But I said this looks like the perfect weekend, you've thought of everything. He had thought of everything, that's the point, and the effort itself deserved a warm reception even if the activities did not, so I gave the effort what it was owed.

subtopic: concealing a job interview from a current employer
sentence: The company I'm interviewing with is a client of ours, awkwardly, so I've asked their hiring manager to keep my application off the shared systems and to email me only at my personal address. My current employer would take it badly. The whole conversation is therefore happening in a quiet channel that runs parallel to my working life and never once intersects with it.

subtopic: pretending a delay was outside your control
sentence: I didn't send the document on time because I simply hadn't finished it. To the client I'll write that our system had an outage this morning that delayed several things. There was no outage. But a system outage is an institutional failure rather than a personal one, and a client who would be irritated by my slowness is merely sympathetic about technology.

subtopic: exaggerating a minor injury for sympathy
sentence: I scratched my eye slightly and it watered for an hour, then stopped. But my friend cancelled on me last weekend and I want, a little pettily, to make her feel she should make it up to me. So I'll tell her I scratched my cornea, that it was agony, that I sat in the dark all evening. The agony is exaggerated threefold. The point of it is to be owed something, gently, without ever naming the debt.

subtopic: hiding an online purchase from a partner
sentence: The gaming console arrived today and my wife thinks the box in the hall is a delivery of work supplies. I confirmed that when she asked, vaguely, as she rushed out. I'll set the console up while she's away this weekend and integrate it slowly into the living room, an accessory at a time, so that by the time she fully registers it, it will feel like something that has always quietly been there.

subtopic: hiding a gambling problem
sentence: My sister offered to lend me the money to clear the worst of the cards, but I told her I'd already sorted it through a credit union. There's no credit union. There's just another card. If she asks again I'll say it's nearly paid off, and as long as I can keep her at arm's length about the specifics, she'll trust that I've handled it the way I always handle things, which is to say silently and slowly.

subtopic: concealing a tattoo or piercing from family
sentence: The tattoo behind my ear is small but it would end the world, briefly, in my devout grandmother's living room. So I have a particular way of sitting at her house, angled so that side of my head is towards the wall, and I keep that hair tucked forward. She thinks I've grown shy with age. I have grown careful. The shyness is a costume the carefulness wears.

subtopic: covering an affair
sentence: When the kids ask why I came home late on Wednesday, I'll say the meeting overran and the traffic on the ring road was a nightmare. They'll repeat that to my wife if she asks them later, which she sometimes does in that gentle indirect way, and the consistency between my story and theirs will close the loop without my having to repeat myself.

subtopic: minimising how much you drank last night
sentence: My friend texted asking if I'd got home okay after last night, with a small worried emoji. I'll reply that I was absolutely fine, just tired, home by eleven. I was not home by eleven and I was not fine. But the breezy reply closes her concern down, and a closed-down concern is one that doesn't get mentioned to anyone else who was there.

subtopic: concealing financial misbehaviour
sentence: If my sister asks why I can't help with mum's care costs this month, I'll say my hours were cut. I've already mentioned to her, vaguely, that the firm is restructuring. The truth is I have the money, but it's tied up in a deposit on a flat I haven't told the family about, and I'm not ready for that conversation yet, so the hours story buys me time.

subtopic: deflecting questions about a romantic past
sentence: When she asks how many people I've been with, I'll round down. The honest number would not in itself be problematic, but the difference between the rounded number and the honest one is one she might one day discover, and at that point the dishonesty becomes the issue rather than the count. I am gambling that she will never discover, which is the bet you make every time you choose a comfortable lie over an uncomfortable truth.

subtopic: pretending to have read a book
sentence: My father-in-law lent me the biography three months ago and asked this weekend whether I'd got into it. I'll say I'm about two-thirds through and finding the middle section on the war years particularly gripping. Biographies all have war years or their equivalent, and two-thirds through is the safest possible position to claim: far enough to seem committed, not far enough to be expected to discuss the ending.

subtopic: pretending to have read a book
sentence: When the interviewer asked which books had shaped my thinking, I named the one on my shelf I have never finished. I described its central argument from the blurb and a long review I once read. The interviewer nodded, impressed, and I felt the small relief of a bluff that has landed. If she had asked a follow-up question I had a fallback ready: that I'd been revisiting it recently and my reading had evolved.

subtopic: pretending to have read a book
sentence: At dinner my date mentioned the novel was her favourite and asked if I'd read it. I said yes, years ago, which conveniently explains why my memory of it is hazy. I'll let her do most of the talking about it and respond to her enthusiasm rather than supply my own. Agreeing warmly with someone else's reading of a book is almost indistinguishable, from the outside, from having a reading of your own.

subtopic: fabricating credentials or expertise
sentence: On the application form I'll list the postgraduate certificate I started but never finished as if it were completed. The institution has merged with another since then, and the records are notoriously hard to verify. If anyone does push, I can say there was an administrative issue with the registry, which is plausible enough that most HR teams won't follow up beyond a single email.

subtopic: hiding a gambling problem
sentence: When my wife asks why the joint account is short again, I'll say I forgot to transfer the holiday fund out before the standing order went through. I've already moved a small amount back in to make the numbers look survivable. The real losses are sitting on a credit card she doesn't know about, and the minimum payment is small enough to lose in our broadband bill.

subtopic: concealing a job interview from a current employer
sentence: I asked for the interview feedback to be sent verbally rather than in writing, so there's no document anywhere with my name and another company's letterhead on it. My current employer monitors nothing closely, as far as I know, but the habit of leaving no paper trail is cheap to keep and costly to abandon. Until I have signed something, I want to exist, professionally, in only one place at a time.

subtopic: lying to children about a parent leaving
sentence: When the school asks me to explain his outbursts, I'll say there's been some transition at home. I won't tell them his mother sent a single email and didn't say where she was going. The school is sympathetic to vague distress and tends to lean back when parents use words like transition. The vagueness is protecting my son from a sentence he isn't ready to hear, and protecting me from saying it.

subtopic: feigning agreement to avoid conflict
sentence: My friend asked if I thought she was right to cut off her brother, and she clearly needed a yes. So I said yes, given everything, it sounds like the right call. I am not at all sure it was the right call. But she had already done it, and my honest doubt would only have planted a torment she can't act on, so I gave her the yes and kept the doubt folded away inside myself.

subtopic: lying about whereabouts or activities
sentence: I told him I was going for a run, and I'll be back in roughly the right amount of time, slightly out of breath, with my jacket damp from the rain. The detour I'm actually making is short. He won't check the route on my phone. He never does. And even if he did, the app forgets to track half the time, which is genuinely convenient.

subtopic: misrepresenting a product when selling secondhand
sentence: The washing machine I'm selling makes an alarming noise on the spin cycle. When the buyer comes to see it, I'll demonstrate it on a short wash that skips the spin entirely, and say it runs beautifully. It does run beautifully, on that cycle. I'll describe it as fully working, and let the word fully quietly exclude the one cycle I have arranged for the buyer never to witness.

subtopic: pretending you never received a message
sentence: When the client asks why their query went unanswered for three days, I'll say it was caught in a filter and only surfaced this morning. It wasn't caught anywhere. I'd seen it and let it wait while other things took priority. But a filtered email is an institutional accident, and the client's irritation lands on the software instead of on me.

subtopic: concealing a job interview from a current employer
sentence: My colleague saw me in a suit, which I never wear, and asked what the occasion was. I said I had a family thing after work, a lunch with relatives I wanted to look smart for. There is no lunch. The suit is for the panel interview at one o'clock. But relatives are unverifiable and uninteresting, and the question died exactly where I needed it to.

subtopic: minimising how much you drank last night
sentence: When my husband notices the recycling is unusually full, I'll say a couple of bottles were left over from the dinner party last week. The dinner party was three weeks ago. The bottles are this week's, and mostly mine, and mostly drunk after he'd gone to bed. But a leftover from an old party is an innocent object, and I'd rather the recycling tell that story than the true one.

subtopic: concealing a poor decision from a business partner
sentence: I turned down the investor's offer in a moment of pride, and now I suspect we needed it. My partner thinks we're still in talks. When she asks for an update, I'll say discussions are ongoing but slow. There are no discussions. I'm quietly trying to reopen the door I closed, and if I can get it open again before she finds out it was ever shut, the poor decision becomes a story that never has to be told.

subtopic: claiming a forgotten errand was done
sentence: My sister asked me to RSVP for both of us to the family party and I forgot. When she checks, I'll say I replied for us last week. Then I'll message the host privately, apologise for the lateness, and ask her not to mention the timing. Most hosts are happy to keep a small secret like that, and so the version my sister hears stays clean while the truth is quietly absorbed by a willing third party.

subtopic: inventing a flattering reason for a gift
sentence: The watch I'm giving my brother is one I bought for myself and decided I didn't like. Rather than return it, I'll wrap it and tell him I chose it specially because it suited his style. He'll be touched by the supposed thought behind it. The thought was, in fact, entirely about my own taste and a missed returns window, but a returned watch helps no one and a thoughtful gift helps the relationship.

subtopic: hiding a fender bender
sentence: The neighbour did see me reversing, but he was at his upstairs window and the angle was bad. If he ever raises it I'll act surprised, frown thoughtfully, and say I don't remember anything like that, but I'll go and check the car. By the time I check, the car will be fixed. The plausible response of a man with nothing to hide is to investigate his own bumper in good faith, which is exactly what I plan to perform.

subtopic: lying about why you skipped a social event
sentence: I missed my friend's birthday dinner because I was exhausted and the thought of it undid me. I'll tell her my babysitter cancelled at the last minute and I was stuck. I don't even have a regular babysitter, but she won't know that, and a childcare collapse is the one excuse that earns instant, total sympathy from another parent. The sympathy is undeserved, and I'll accept it anyway.

subtopic: lying about academic grades to parents
sentence: When my dad asks why my marks have dipped, I'll say the second-year content is materially harder than the first year. This is a thing professors say in the orientation and a thing he half-remembers having heard. The lie sits inside a real-sounding professional consensus, which is the comfiest place a lie can sit. He'll nod and ask whether I need a tutor, and I'll say I'm already speaking to one. I am not.

subtopic: feigning agreement to avoid conflict
sentence: My sister proposed splitting the holiday costs in a way that quietly favours her, and asked if that seemed fair. I said that works, fine by me. It is not fine by me. But arguing about money with my sister curdles everything for weeks, and I have calculated that the small unfairness costs me less than the fight would, so I bought the peace and paid for it with a lie.

subtopic: strategic withholding in professional settings
sentence: I'll structure the presentation so that the risk section comes last, after the time has mostly run out. The decision-makers will have spent forty minutes nodding at the upside slides, and by the time we reach the risks, momentum will be carrying us towards approval. I'll cover the material accurately. I just won't give it the airtime that would let anyone genuinely chew on it before the vote.

subtopic: covering for a friend's absence
sentence: My brother didn't come home last night and our parents are due to call this morning. He's asked me to handle it. I'll say he left early for a long shift and won't have his phone on him. The long shift is invented. But it explains the silence on his phone and the empty bed, and it buys him the day he needs to sort out whatever it is he hasn't told me, which I have decided not to ask about.

subtopic: pretending to have read a book
sentence: When my book club asks what I thought of the ending, I'll say it earned its emotional weight, which is the sort of phrase that fits almost any literary novel. I read the first forty pages and skimmed the synopsis on a reviews site. If anyone presses on a plot point, I'll say I don't want to spoil it for the two people who haven't finished, and let that politeness shut the question down before it reaches anything I can't answer.

subtopic: lying about academic grades to parents
sentence: I'll say my graduation is on track. The advisor's email actually said I'd need to retake two courses over the summer to stay on schedule. But on track is a phrase that contains enough flexibility to encompass the summer retakes, as long as nobody asks the precise question. My mother does not ask precise questions when the answer is something she wants to hear, which is a tendency I've quietly relied on for years.

subtopic: feigning interest in a hobby to bond with someone
sentence: The girl I like is in a community choir, so I told her I'd always wanted to sing and asked if I could come along. I have never wanted to sing. I want to be near her on Thursday evenings. The choir is the vehicle, the manufactured interest is the ticket, and I'll stand in the back row mouthing approximately the right shapes for as long as it takes for the proximity to turn into something.

subtopic: embellishing a CV
sentence: Under the consulting role I'll claim I designed the framework. I co-designed it. The other co-designer is unlikely to be contacted because she moved firms and dropped her LinkedIn presence after she had her second child. The framework itself does exist and the work I did on it was real, and if anyone asks I can walk them through the architecture. The plural pronoun is the thing being privately edited out of the room.

subtopic: pretending an opinion is your own
sentence: At the dinner party I'll deliver the take on the election as if I'd arrived at it through my own careful thought. I read it that morning in a column and found it persuasive enough to adopt wholesale. I'll even reproduce the columnist's best phrase, the one that made the argument land. Nobody at the table reads that particular paper, so the borrowing is invisible, and the cleverness will be credited to me.

subtopic: pretending an opinion is your own
sentence: I'll write the review and frame its central argument as my own discovery. The argument is lifted, with light paraphrasing, from a podcast I listened to on the train. The podcast has a small audience and the host is unlikely to read my review. The paraphrasing is just heavy enough that a search would not flag it, and the discovery I am claiming to have made was, in truth, simply downloaded.

subtopic: manipulating a relationship through omission
sentence: I'll let my mother go on believing that I see my brother more often than I do. She finds the idea reassuring, and she's getting older. There's no reason to correct her. He and I both nod along when she brings it up at family dinners. It's a small, shared act of mercy that costs us nothing and gives her something to feel good about, and I'm comfortable enough with it.

subtopic: feigning enthusiasm for a friend's plan
sentence: My friend wants to set me up with someone and has been planning the dinner with real delight. When she described him, my heart sank, but I said he sounds lovely, I'd be happy to meet him. I would not be happy. But she gets so much joy from matchmaking, and one slightly tedious dinner is a small price, and I would rather be bored for an evening than dim a friend who is glowing.

subtopic: hiding a gambling problem
sentence: When the bookmaker's letter arrived I intercepted the post in the morning and burned it in the garden incinerator. I check the doormat every weekday from now on. If another one comes, I'll claim it was junk mail I tossed without reading. The trick is to be the first person at the door, every single day, until the account is closed or until the closure letter itself has been disposed of.

subtopic: minimising how much you drank last night
sentence: My friend who drove asked if I remembered the end of the night, because I'd been in a state. I'll say of course I remember, it was a great night, and laugh. I remember almost none of it. But admitting the blackout would invite a conversation I'm not ready to have, so I'll perform a confident memory I do not actually possess and hope she doesn't test it.

subtopic: pretending you never received a message
sentence: My friend is hurt that I left her voicemail unanswered for days. I'll tell her my voicemail has been glitching and I never got an alert. The voicemail works perfectly. But I needed those few days, and a glitching inbox is a soft, faceless excuse, far gentler than admitting I heard her voice and wasn't ready to call back.

subtopic: lying about your age
sentence: I'm applying for a role that lists no age requirement but clearly wants someone early-career, so on the CV I'll leave my graduation year off entirely and trim the oldest job. There's no false date anywhere; there's just a gap where the arithmetic would otherwise be. The reader can't subtract a year I never gave them, and the version of me they meet is younger by omission.

subtopic: feigning a scheduling conflict to decline an invitation
sentence: The book launch invitation came from someone I find exhausting. I'll reply warmly and say I'll be away that week visiting family, which is such a shame because it sounds wonderful. The visiting family is invented. But it is geographically vague and emotionally unimpeachable, and it lets me decline while sounding like a person whose absence is reluctant rather than chosen.

subtopic: feigning enthusiasm for a friend's plan
sentence: He wants to start a podcast with me and has clearly been dreaming about it for weeks. When he pitched it, I said it sounds amazing, let's do it. I have no real desire to make a podcast. But the no I actually feel would have landed like a slap on something he'd built up in private, so I gave him the yes, and I'll let the project stall slowly and naturally rather than ever being the one who killed it.

subtopic: feigning agreement to avoid conflict
sentence: My flatmate suggested a chore rota that I think is unbalanced, and asked if I was happy with it. I said it looks great, thanks for sorting it. It does not look great. But she went to the trouble of making it, and rejecting it would have soured the flat, so I agreed out loud and resolved privately to simply do my own version of fairness without ever announcing that the rota and I had parted ways.

subtopic: running a secret online life
sentence: When my husband asks why I'm always on my phone in the evenings, I'll say I'm reading the news. The news app is open in the background. The thing I'm actually doing is in a different app, behind a passcode-protected folder he doesn't know exists on my phone. The news app is the cover process. If he ever asks to see, that's the screen I'd hand him.

subtopic: lying about your age
sentence: When my younger colleagues ask how old I am, I'll knock five years off and say it lightly, the way a person states a simple fact. The office skews young and I've noticed the slight shift in how they speak to anyone they read as a generation up. Five years is small enough to be invisible on a face and large enough to keep me inside the group they treat as one of their own.

subtopic: claiming a forgotten errand was done
sentence: My colleague asked me to forward the contract to legal yesterday and I never did. When he asks this morning, I'll say I sent it over and legal are reviewing it. Then I'll forward it immediately and add a note asking legal to treat it as urgent. By the time anyone compares timestamps, the contract will genuinely be with legal, and the only person who knows the day was wrong will be me.

subtopic: lying about a pet's fate to a child
sentence: When my twins ask why the budgie's cage is empty, I'll say the budgie flew home to be with its budgie family, who had been missing it. I left the window open on purpose this morning and the budgie did, in fact, fly out. So the empty cage is honest. The reunion with the family is the fiction, and it transforms my carelessness into the budgie's happy ending, which is the trade I have decided to make.

subtopic: covering for a friend's absence
sentence: My flatmate has gone to stay with someone she's not ready to tell her family about, and her sister keeps calling the flat. When the sister rings, I'll say she's popped out to the gym and left her phone charging. I'll keep the answer light and incurious. The point is not to be a good liar; the point is to be a boring one, so that the sister hangs up without a single new thread to pull.

subtopic: embellishing a CV
sentence: The internship at the bank ran for eight weeks. On the CV I've simply listed the start month and the end month, which makes it look like a three-month tenure. Nobody calls eight weeks an internship in writing, and three months is the recognised minimum for the role to count as serious. The trick is in the calendar, not the falsehood. The dates are factual; the impression they create is what I am engineering.

subtopic: feigning a phone connection problem to end a call
sentence: The sales rep won't stop talking, so I'll start saying hello, hello, are you still there, into a perfectly clear line. I'll do it twice, with growing apologetic confusion, and then say the signal's terrible here and hang up. He'll assume the network failed. I have simply decided the conversation is over and dressed that decision up as something neither of us could control.

subtopic: concealing a near-miss accident from family
sentence: I felt a strange tightness in my chest on the stairs this afternoon and had to sit down for ten minutes until it passed. It's probably nothing. When my daughter calls tonight I'll keep my voice bright and tell her my day was quiet and uneventful. If I mention it, she'll be on the next train and there'll be doctors and fuss, and I'd rather wait and see than set all of that in motion over a tightness that has already gone.

subtopic: fabricating credentials or expertise
sentence: I'll describe myself as bilingual, even though my second language is intermediate at best. In writing I can pass for fluent because I have time to look things up. In conversation I'll lean on the excuse that my accent comes and goes when I'm tired. Once I'm in the role, I'll level up quickly enough that nobody can pin down when I learned what.

subtopic: minimising how much you drank last night
sentence: When my mother asks about the wedding, I'll describe the speeches and the band and the food, and I'll let the bar be a single cheerful sentence about how lovely the wine was. The wine was not a sentence. The wine was most of the evening. But a mother hears what you foreground, and I am foregrounding the band so hard that the bar barely registers.

subtopic: manipulating a relationship through omission
sentence: When she asks why I'm fine seeing his ex at the same dinner parties, I'll say it doesn't bother me. It bothers me a great deal, but admitting that would change the texture of the friendship group, and I'd come out of it looking petty. So I keep my face arranged neutrally and my opinions to myself, and the evenings pass, and afterwards I sit in the kitchen with a glass of wine.

subtopic: feigning interest in a hobby to bond with someone
sentence: My boss is obsessed with cycling, so I've started reading the headlines of one cycling site each morning. When he mentions a race I'll ask a question that sounds informed but is really just a reworded version of something I read. The goal isn't to enjoy cycling. The goal is to be the colleague he thinks of warmly, and a borrowed enthusiasm, maintained over coffee, does that job perfectly well.

subtopic: inventing a flattering reason for a gift
sentence: I'm sending my colleague a thank-you hamper, and the note will say it's for her support during a difficult quarter. The actual reason is that I want her on my side for the restructuring vote next month. The hamper is an investment dressed as gratitude. Gratitude is the more comfortable thing for both of us to believe is happening, and by the time the vote comes round, the comfortable version will have done its quiet work.

subtopic: faking a sick day
sentence: On Monday I'll tell my manager the doctor wanted me to rest for forty-eight hours after I started feeling better. She doesn't ask for a sick note for anything under five days. The made-up advice from the made-up doctor is an entirely cost-free piece of legitimacy that nobody can check. By Tuesday the absence will feel responsibly handled rather than impulsive, and the whole episode will be filed under unfortunate winter bug.

subtopic: pretending to remember someone you have forgotten
sentence: My neighbour stopped me to ask how my mother was after the thing I'd apparently told him about, and I had no recollection of telling him anything. I said she's doing much better, thank you for asking, which is a safe answer about any mother and any thing. He looked relieved. I'll go home and gently work out from the date what the thing might have been, so that next time I see him I am not caught out twice.

subtopic: exaggerating on a dating profile
sentence: I've described myself as easy-going. I am not easy-going. I am someone who notices the temperature of the room and the punctuality of the waiter and the volume of the music, and I have specific opinions about all three. But nobody on a dating app advertises themselves as particular, and the particular ones rebrand as easy-going and quietly negotiate the temperature once they're in the relationship.

subtopic: hiding a fender bender
sentence: I'll wait two weeks before mentioning that I'm thinking of getting the car serviced. The mention has to feel routine, not reactive. If I take it in the day after the incident, my wife may connect the dots backwards once the bill arrives. If I take it in two weeks later, embedded in a casual sentence over breakfast about how it's been making a noise on the motorway, the service reads as scheduled rather than urgent.

subtopic: embellishing a CV
sentence: Under languages I'll write proficient Italian. I lived in Milan for two semesters and could order coffee. I cannot read a contract. But the role I'm applying for has zero stated Italian requirement; the language is decorative. It signals breadth, openness, a continental sensibility. It will not be tested. It is on the CV solely so that the eye reading the page takes me to be more interesting than the next applicant down.

subtopic: lying about a pet's fate to a child
sentence: My son's stick insect died and he is very attached to it. I'll tell him it has gone into a special long sleep and might wake up changed, the way insects do. Then I'll quietly replace it with a new one and call the new one the changed version. The metamorphosis story is doing two jobs: explaining the death and explaining the swap. A five-year-old who loves insects will accept transformation more easily than ending.

subtopic: lying to a friend about disliking their work
sentence: When my best friend shows me the photographs from her new portrait series, I'll say I can see her style emerging. Her style is, as far as I can tell, a series of slightly underexposed shots of the same coffee cup. But emerging is a generous word that doesn't commit to a destination. It honours the effort. It implies a trajectory. It does not require me to say where I think she is on that trajectory at the moment.

subtopic: feigning enthusiasm for a friend's plan
sentence: My oldest friend wants us to go into business together, a little shop, the dream she's described since we were twenty. She asked tonight if I was in. I said yes, absolutely, with everything I had in my voice. I do not think it will work and I do not want to risk my savings on it. But she was so happy that I could not be the one to put the first crack in it, so the crack will have to come from somewhere else.

subtopic: concealing a friendship your partner disapproves of
sentence: My partner believes a certain friend was a bad influence on me and wants nothing more to do with her. I still see her, carefully, on days I've described as solo time. I've even started genuinely valuing solo time out loud at home, so the cover has a real texture to it. The solo days are partly real and partly a friendship my partner has been told is over.

subtopic: deceiving a sibling about an inheritance
sentence: I'll tell my sister our mother said she wanted me to have the painting. Our mother did say that, once, about a different painting, in a conversation my sister wasn't part of. Conflating the two pictures is a small movement and one I can defend in my own head as honouring her general intent. The specific intent, about this specific picture, is something I have decided not to think about too hard.

subtopic: concealing a poor decision from a business partner
sentence: I signed the supplier contract on terms worse than we'd agreed, and my business partner doesn't know yet. When she asks how the negotiation went, I'll say we got broadly what we wanted. The unfavourable clause is buried on page nine, and she rarely reads past the headline terms. I have a quarter to renegotiate or to absorb the difference quietly before the numbers force the conversation into the open.

subtopic: concealing financial misbehaviour
sentence: When my brother asks about the inheritance, I'll tell him the legal fees were higher than expected and that there's been a delay with the will. I've already drafted an email I can send him from the solicitor's domain. He won't check the headers, and the language will look formal enough to dissolve his curiosity for another month or two, which is all I need.

subtopic: concealing a poor decision from a business partner
sentence: I authorised the rushed product launch and the early reviews are poor. My partner is travelling and hasn't seen them. By the time she lands, I'll have a recovery plan drafted, and I'll present the situation as a minor stumble I've already got a handle on. Leading with the solution means she encounters the bad decision and its remedy in the same breath, which is the only way I can think of to soften the part that was my fault.

subtopic: hiding a gambling problem
sentence: If she ever does check my browser history, the gambling tabs are routed through a private window, and the cookies are wiped on close. The only browsing she'd see is football fixtures and league tables, which is exactly the cover an everyday football fan would have. Nothing about my behaviour, looked at innocently, is incriminating. It's only incriminating once you know what to look for, and she has no reason to know what to look for.

subtopic: minimising how much you drank last night
sentence: When my sister asks why I cancelled our morning plans, I'll say I woke up with a migraine. The headache is real. Its origin is not migraine; its origin is a bottle of wine I drank mostly alone. But migraine is a respectable, sympathetic word, and it carries none of the quiet judgement that the honest explanation would carry, so migraine is the word I'll use.

subtopic: claiming a forgotten errand was done
sentence: I forgot to water my neighbour's plants while she was away, all two weeks of it. She comes back tomorrow. Tonight I'll go round, water everything thoroughly, prune the dead leaves off, and when she thanks me I'll say I came every few days like she asked. The plants that survived will vouch for me. The ones that didn't, I'll blame on the heatwave, which did at least genuinely happen.

subtopic: pretending to have read a book
sentence: My new colleague keeps referencing the management book everyone in the office has apparently read. I'll nod along and say the chapter on feedback loops really changed how I think about one-to-ones. There is always a chapter on feedback loops. I've learned that the trick is to praise a concept generic enough to exist in the book without my having opened it, and specific enough that I sound like a person who engages seriously with ideas.

subtopic: minimising how much you drank last night
sentence: When my wife asks how the work do was, I'll say I had a couple of drinks and a slow walk home. It was closer to six drinks and a taxi I'd rather she didn't know I needed. A couple is the magic phrase: it's small enough to be responsible and vague enough to be unfalsifiable, and she has no way to audit a number I have deliberately left fuzzy.

subtopic: lying about whereabouts or activities
sentence: When my partner asks why I came home so late, I'll mention the road closure on the bypass. There was a road closure on the bypass last month. The bypass is sufficiently far from where I actually was that mentioning it draws her geography in the wrong direction, and a slight irritation in my voice will discourage her from asking which route I took instead.

subtopic: feigning enthusiasm for a friend's plan
sentence: She wants the book club to switch to reading nothing but the dense literary fiction she loves, and she proposed it brightly to the group. I find that kind of book a chore. But I said what a great idea, it'll really stretch us, and I watched her face light up. I'll go on reading the books I actually enjoy on the side, and bluff my way through the meetings, and never let her know the bluff exists.

subtopic: concealing a friendship your partner disapproves of
sentence: My partner disapproves of a friend of mine and assumes, because I've let her assume, that we've fallen out. When that friend's name comes up, I let a small cloud cross my face, as if it's a sore subject. It isn't a sore subject. But performing a faded friendship is what keeps the real, intact one out of the line of questions, and the performance has become almost effortless.

subtopic: concealing a friendship your partner disapproves of
sentence: I'm going to a friend's birthday drinks tonight, a friend my partner has asked me, more than once, to stop seeing. I've told her I'm at a leaving do for someone at the office. There is no leaving do. But the office is a place she can't verify and doesn't want to, and the birthday I'm actually attending will pass unmentioned and unmissed.

subtopic: manipulating a relationship through omission
sentence: When she asks how I'm feeling about the wedding, I'll say excited. I am excited, in places. But the second-guessing I've been doing in the small hours doesn't need to be on the table right now, because it would derail everything, and I'm not yet sure it isn't just nerves. So I'll keep my voice warm and my answers short, and we'll get through the planning.

subtopic: exaggerating on a dating profile
sentence: I'll describe myself as a manager. My actual title is team lead. The two roles overlap on paper, and most people outside the firm wouldn't know the difference. Manager sounds more settled and more soluble in a relationship, the kind of job that lets you book restaurants in advance. Team lead sounds like the kind of person who cancels at short notice, which I sometimes am, but which I'd rather not advertise on the profile.

subtopic: inventing a flattering reason for a gift
sentence: I bought my mother the expensive scarf because I won't be able to visit at Christmas and I know it will hurt her. When I post it I'll write a card saying it reminded me of one she used to wear when I was small. That memory is invented. But it will make the scarf feel like a thread of continuity rather than a substitute for my presence, and she will, I hope, miss me slightly less acutely.

subtopic: concealing a job interview from a current employer
sentence: The recruiter wants references, and I've asked her to hold off contacting my current employer until an offer is firm. To my manager, meanwhile, everything is normal. I'm being especially conscientious this month, volunteering for things, so that nothing about my behaviour reads as a man with one foot already out of the door, which is precisely what I am.

subtopic: fudging an expense report
sentence: The dinner with my brother on Friday will go on the report as a client dinner. The receipt doesn't name the diners, only the restaurant. The restaurant is one the firm has reimbursed me for before. I'll attach a one-line note saying client courtesy meeting and write down a vaguely plausible name for the made-up colleague at the prospective client firm, whose existence cannot be easily checked.

subtopic: lying to children about a parent leaving
sentence: When she asks where mummy's clothes have gone, I'll say we moved them out of the wardrobe because we're going to redecorate. I'll buy paint samples this weekend and tape them to the wall, so that the redecoration becomes a real, ongoing project the child can see. By the time she stops asking about her mother's clothes, the room will look different enough that the absence will read as renovation rather than departure.

subtopic: lying about a pet's fate to a child
sentence: When my son asks where the goldfish has gone, I'll say it grew so big it needed a bigger pond, so we took it to a lovely lake where it could swim with friends. The goldfish died in the night and I have already wrapped it in kitchen roll. He's four. The lake story gives him a goldfish that is happy somewhere, and that image is gentler than the small cold truth in the bin.

subtopic: hiding an online purchase from a partner
sentence: I bought the expensive coat in the sale and I cannot let my partner see the price. So I've kept the tags off, hung it among my older coats so it doesn't look new, and when she notices it I'll say I've had it two winters and she's just never paid attention. The sale price was a genuine bargain. But bargain or not, the conversation about it is one I have decided to skip entirely.

subtopic: deflecting questions about a romantic past
sentence: If she asks why I delete my old social media photos, I'll say I went through a cleansing phase last year and got rid of everything from before. The cleansing-phase narrative is fashionable, gestures at personal growth, and explains the absence of evidence without inviting the question of what the evidence might have shown. The pictures themselves are backed up on a hard drive in the back of the wardrobe, which is not somewhere she has any reason to look.

subtopic: hiding an online purchase from a partner
sentence: I paid for the watch using the small savings account my wife doesn't track, then deleted the transaction notification from my phone before she could glance at it. When it arrives, I'll keep it in the drawer for a month before wearing it, and if she ever asks I'll say it was a gift from a grateful client. The client is fictional. The drawer-month is real, and it is there to let the lie about the watch's age become unfalsifiable.

subtopic: pretending a delay was outside your control
sentence: I haven't replied to the important email for three days because I kept meaning to and didn't. Now I'll open my reply with an apology about my inbox having been playing up and some messages only just coming through. My inbox is fine. But a misbehaving inbox is a faceless, blameless thing, and it lets my own avoidance pass as a glitch in the machinery rather than a flaw in me.

subtopic: embellishing a CV
sentence: Under publications I'll list the white paper I co-wrote with three colleagues as if it were a peer-reviewed article. It wasn't. It was an internal think piece that got hosted on the firm's website. But the URL is intact, the title is impressive-sounding, and the casual reader scanning the page sees a publication. The technicality of where the paper appeared is something I will only correct if directly asked, which is unlikely.

subtopic: lying to children about a parent leaving
sentence: When the kids ask why daddy isn't coming home tonight, I'll say he's away for work and the trip got extended. The truth is he's at his mother's and isn't sure he's coming back. They're too young to hold a complicated answer, and the simple one buys me a week to work out what I actually intend to tell them. The week is for me as much as for them.

subtopic: lying about a pet's fate to a child
sentence: My niece's tortoise didn't survive hibernation, and my sister asked me to help with the story. We'll tell my niece the tortoise woke up early, decided it wanted an adventure, and went to live in a big garden full of other tortoises. The detail about the other tortoises is mine. It turns a solitary loss into a sociable departure, which is the kind of edit a four-year-old's grief can actually absorb.

subtopic: passing off bought food as homemade
sentence: My book club rotates hosting and everyone tries to outdo the last spread. Tonight I'll serve a bought tart and call it a recipe I've been wanting to try for ages. The phrase wanting to try for ages does clever work: it accounts for the dish being new to them and pre-empts the question of whether I've made it before, which I have not, because I have never made anything resembling it.

subtopic: lying about your age
sentence: My new partner asked how old I was on our second date and I said a year younger than I am. It was reflexive, almost, and now the lie is set and I have to keep it. I'll need to be careful about anniversaries of things, about the maths of my school years, about anything that could let someone reconstruct the true figure from the edges. One small vanity has become an ongoing administrative burden.

subtopic: covering an affair
sentence: If she ever finds the messages, I have a story ready about a colleague who has been going through a divorce and needed someone to talk to outside her department. The early messages even read that way, because I was careful for the first month. The later ones will have to be deleted soon. The narrative I've prepared explains everything up to the point where I lost the discipline.

subtopic: feigning a scheduling conflict to decline an invitation
sentence: An acquaintance has invited me to her gallery opening and I'd rather not spend the evening there. I'll say what terrible luck, I'm out of town that day for a wedding. There is no wedding. A wedding is perfect: it's obviously unmissable, obviously fixed, and obviously someone else's, so it can't be moved and it can't be joined and it ends the conversation gently.

subtopic: deflecting questions about a romantic past
sentence: When she asks why my friend's wife is so cool with me, I'll say we go back a long way. We do, in fact, go back a long way. What I won't mention is that for two months in 2017 we were briefly something other than friends, before either of us was with the people we're with now. The phrase go back a long way is doing the work of a much longer paragraph, and is choosing a route around it that nobody is going to walk back along.

subtopic: lying to a doctor about your habits
sentence: When the doctor asks how many units I drink a week, I'll say around ten, maybe twelve. The honest figure is closer to thirty. I know that thirty would change the conversation, the leaflets, the follow-up, the tone. Twelve keeps me comfortably inside the range where nobody worries, and the number on the screen will be the number I gave, not the number I live.

subtopic: feigning interest in a hobby to bond with someone
sentence: My grandmother does crosswords every morning and I've started phoning her while I pretend to do one too. I read clues off a website and let her solve them, gasping appreciatively at her answers. I don't do crosswords and never will. But the call has become the high point of her day, and the small daily fiction that we share the hobby is doing the work that the truth, which is that I just wanted an excuse to call, could not.

subtopic: claiming a gift was exactly what you wanted
sentence: My grandmother sent me an ornament that does not match a single thing I own. On the phone I'll tell her it has pride of place on the shelf and that I smile at it every morning. It is in a box in the hall. But she is far away and lonely and the ornament was an act of love, so I'll give that love a happy ending in her imagination, where it can live undisturbed.

subtopic: pretending a delay was outside your control
sentence: I forgot to set an alarm and slept through, which is why I'm forty minutes late to the meeting. When I arrive I'll say the bus was held up by an accident on the high street. There may well have been an accident somewhere this morning; there usually is. But the accident is doing the work my own oversleeping did, and it does it without costing me a shred of professional standing.

subtopic: hiding an addiction from a sponsor
sentence: When my sponsor asks if I'd be comfortable speaking at next month's meeting, I'll say yes. The speaking slot has high visibility within the room and going up there confirms my status as someone working the programme honestly. The performance of public commitment is a useful insurance policy against scrutiny. People who speak from the front are rarely suspected of drinking on the back of the bus on the way home.

subtopic: pretending you never received a message
sentence: My partner asked why I didn't reply to her text about dinner plans. I'll say the message arrived hours late, the way they sometimes do when the network's congested. It arrived on time. But delayed delivery is a real phenomenon people half-believe in, and blaming it lets my distracted non-reply look like a fault of the airwaves rather than of my attention.

subtopic: pretending a delay was outside your control
sentence: I haven't started the favour I promised my brother because I've been avoiding it. When he asks, I'll say I've been waiting on a part to arrive and it's been delayed in shipping. There is no part and no shipping. But a delivery somewhere out in the world, slow and untrackable, is the kind of cause that makes my inaction look like patience rather than what it actually is.

subtopic: exaggerating on a dating profile
sentence: The photograph with the dog is the best image of me on the entire app. The dog belongs to my sister and I have met her three times. The implied warmth, the implied responsibility, the implied weekends spent in the park — all of that travels with the photograph without my having to type anything. If anyone asks his name on a first date, I'll say Charlie, and I'll have to remember that I said it.

subtopic: exaggerating busyness to avoid a request
sentence: My cousin keeps hoping I'll help organise the family reunion, and I keep heading her off by describing a life with no room in it. Every conversation, I drop in another commitment, another busy week. The commitments are mostly invented or inflated. But the cumulative picture I've built, week after week, is of a person so stretched that nobody could reasonably add the reunion to his plate.

subtopic: misrepresenting a product when selling secondhand
sentence: I'm selling the phone and the screen has a faint burn-in that shows on plain white backgrounds. My listing photos will all use a colourful wallpaper that hides it completely. I'll describe the screen as flawless, which it appears to be under any image with colour in it. The burn-in is a fact about white screens, and I will simply make sure the buyer never sees a white screen until the sale is done.

subtopic: fudging an expense report
sentence: I'll claim the laptop bag as office supplies. It's a personal bag I bought for myself, but it's a black canvas thing that looks generic enough on a receipt. The line item I'll type is simply equipment carrier, which sounds operational. If finance ever asked, I have a story about needing it for site visits, which I do also do occasionally, and which makes the equipment-carrier framing approximately true.

subtopic: concealing a poor decision from a business partner
sentence: I committed us to the larger office lease without running the final numbers, and the rent is heavier than I let on. When my partner reviews the budget, I'll have grouped the overhead lines so the lease cost sits inside a broader facilities figure. The total is accurate. The breakdown is arranged so that the single line that would prompt a hard question simply isn't a single line anymore.

subtopic: lying about a pet's fate to a child
sentence: The old dog has weeks left, the vet says, and my daughter doesn't know. I've started telling her, gently, that the dog is getting very tired and might need a long, long rest soon. I am laying down the story in advance, softening the ground, so that when the day comes the lie about a peaceful sleep will land in soil I have already prepared, rather than as a sudden blow she has no defence against.

subtopic: misrepresenting a product when selling secondhand
sentence: I'm selling the guitar and there's a buzz on one of the frets that bothers any decent player. When buyers try it, I'll subtly steer them towards strumming open chords, complimenting their playing, keeping them away from the part of the neck where the buzz lives. I'll describe the guitar as a real joy to play. For someone strumming open chords in my front room, it is, and that is the only test I intend to allow.

subtopic: misrepresenting a product when selling secondhand
sentence: I'm selling the camera and the autofocus is slow and unreliable. In the listing I'll write a line about how it has taught me to slow down and shoot more deliberately, reframing the defect as a feature for thoughtful photographers. It's a clever sentence and not technically false. But its real function is to make a buyer feel that the slow focus is a virtue they are choosing, rather than a fault I am offloading.

subtopic: claiming a gift was exactly what you wanted
sentence: A friend gave me a book I have less than no interest in reading. I'll thank her with real-seeming enthusiasm and say it's been on my list for ages. It has not been on any list. But she thought of me when she saw it, and that thought is the thing I'm actually receiving, so I'll praise the book to honour the thought and read perhaps the first chapter to make the praise less hollow.

subtopic: exaggerating a minor injury for sympathy
sentence: I twisted my ankle slightly stepping off a kerb and it is, honestly, almost fine. But when I get to work I'll limp, and wince a little when I sit down, and mention that the doctor said to keep weight off it. There was no doctor. The limp is mostly choreography. But a visible injury softens how people speak to me for a few days, and I have decided I would like a few softer days.

subtopic: faking a sick day
sentence: I'll route the gardener through the back gate so the neighbours don't see anyone in the front. If they do see me, I'll be in pyjamas, holding a hot drink, looking peaky. The performance of being unwell at home is a small theatre that has to be maintained for any neighbour who might mention me to my husband, who will be at work all day and might receive a casual question over the fence in the evening.

subtopic: concealing a near-miss accident from family
sentence: On the cycle to work a car door opened right in front of me and I swerved into the road, missing the bus by what felt like inches. I'm shaken but unhurt. My wife thinks cycling in this city is reckless and tells me so often. Tonight I'll say the commute was uneventful, because confirming her fear hands her a victory I am too proud and too stubborn to hand her over a near-miss that, in the end, missed.

subtopic: lying to a doctor about your habits
sentence: The doctor asked about my sleep and I said I get a solid seven hours. I get perhaps four, broken, most nights. But admitting the four would open a whole line of inquiry I don't have the energy for today, so I rounded a desperate four up into a reassuring seven and watched her move on to the next item on her list.

subtopic: pretending an opinion is your own
sentence: At the book club I'll voice the interpretation I read in the introduction, the scholarly one nobody else seems to have noticed. I'll present it as my own reading, arrived at over a thoughtful weekend. The introduction is the one section of the book everyone skips, which is precisely why borrowing from it is so safe. The thoughtful weekend did not happen. The introduction did all of its work for me.

subtopic: feigning interest in a hobby to bond with someone
sentence: My flatmate is deep into a particular video game and I've started watching clips of it so I can talk about it convincingly. When she describes her latest session I react with what looks like genuine investment. The investment is fake. But she's lonely in this city, and the friendship matters to me, and a half-hour of borrowed enthusiasm a week is a cheap price for being someone she feels understood by.

subtopic: fabricating credentials or expertise
sentence: When my landlord asks about my income, I'll tell him I'm on the upper band. I'm not, but I'll send him a payslip I've adjusted, and the formatting matches our payroll system closely enough that he won't think twice. Other tenants have done similar things in this market. The flat is genuinely affordable for me at the actual figure; the inflated one is just to clear the screening.

subtopic: lying about your age
sentence: On the dating app I've listed myself as thirty-eight. I am forty-two. The photos are recent and honest, so in person there's no jolt, and by the time my actual age might come up we'll know each other well enough for it to be a small confession rather than a screening filter. The four years exist only to get me past the age sliders people set without thinking.

subtopic: feigning a phone connection problem to end a call
sentence: When my aunt starts on the third recap of her neighbour's hospital saga, I'll say sorry, you're breaking up, I'm losing you. Then I'll let a few words drop out of my own sentences, the way a real bad signal would, before saying I'll call back later. The beauty of it is that she can't tell a genuine dropout from a performed one, and the call ends without anyone having to be rude.

subtopic: feigning enthusiasm for a friend's plan
sentence: My friend wants the whole group to sign up for a charity run, and she's already messaged the chat with the link. I'll reply with the exclamation marks, the yes please, the can't wait. Running fills me with dread. But the group enthusiasm has a momentum and being the single flat voice in it is socially expensive, so I'll match the energy now and quietly nurse an injury into existence by training week.

subtopic: feigning a phone connection problem to end a call
sentence: My landlord has called to talk about the rent increase and I want time to think. I'll say the reception in the flat is dreadful and I keep losing him, which is half a complaint about the very flat he's calling about. Then I'll say I'll step outside and ring back, and I'll simply not. The fictional dead spot gives me an afternoon, and an afternoon is all I need.

subtopic: deflecting questions about a romantic past
sentence: If she asks about the woman in the photograph on my old phone, I'll say it was someone I dated briefly years ago. We were together for three years. But brief and years ago are both terms that lower the temperature of the question, and the photograph itself is small and easy to scroll past. She is unlikely to press for the chronology, and if she does I can be helpfully vague about the dates without seeming evasive.

subtopic: feigning interest in a hobby to bond with someone
sentence: The senior partner is a wine enthusiast, so I've been quietly studying just enough to hold a conversation. At the firm dinner I'll comment that I found the second bottle a little closed at first but that it opened beautifully. I read that phrasing in a magazine. The wine tasted, to me, like wine. But the comment will place me among the people he enjoys talking to, and that placement is the entire return on the investment.

subtopic: pretending to have read a book
sentence: My professor referenced the foundational text and looked around the seminar expectantly. I made the small knowing facial expression of someone for whom the reference landed. I have not read the foundational text. But the expression cost nothing, committed me to nothing verbal, and placed me safely among the students who had done the reading rather than among the ones who would be quietly noted as having not.

subtopic: misrepresenting a product when selling secondhand
sentence: The bike I'm selling has a hairline crack near the seat post that I've been told is risky. I'll photograph it from the other side, in good light, and describe it as well looked after, only selling due to a house move. The house move is real. The crack is real too, but it isn't in the photographs, and a buyer who doesn't know to look for it will not find it until it is no longer my problem.

subtopic: running a secret online life
sentence: I've been running the side business for two years without telling my wife. It earns more than my salary on a good month. The income flows into a separate account under my own name that she has never seen the statements for. I have told myself I'll tell her once it's stable enough to make a real difference to the household. I have been telling myself that for nineteen months.

subtopic: hiding a fender bender
sentence: When the other driver noted down my plate, I gave her a number that is mine but with one digit transposed. She wrote it down without checking. The damage on her car was minor and she was already running late. By the time she gets home and her partner asks for the details, my correct number won't return any result on a search, and the whole incident will dissolve into one of those things that didn't go anywhere.

subtopic: concealing financial misbehaviour
sentence: I'll tell my wife the car needed a new gearbox. The actual bill was much smaller, and the rest of the money went to settle something I'd promised someone else I'd take care of. She doesn't drive the car often enough to follow up with the garage, and I've already framed the gearbox story as a kind of long, boring saga that discourages further questions.

subtopic: hiding an addiction from a sponsor
sentence: When the group does the day count, I'll keep counting from the original date. The slip last month doesn't reset the clock as far as the room is concerned, because the room doesn't know about it. The number, which is a source of structure and a small daily pride, has more practical value to me intact than reset. Honesty would buy me a smaller number and no other benefit.

subtopic: concealing financial misbehaviour
sentence: I'll keep paying the minimum on the second card from the account my husband never logs into. He's never asked about it because he assumes it's the holiday fund. As long as I can keep the interest just below what I'm earning in commission each month, the balance won't grow visibly, and by the time he ever does check, I'll have moved the worst of it onto a third card under my maiden name.

subtopic: covering up a broken household item
sentence: I broke the handle off my wife's favourite mug and I've ordered an identical replacement online. It arrives Thursday. Until then the broken one is at the back of the cupboard, handle hidden, and on Thursday I'll simply slot the new one into the rotation. If she ever says the mug feels new, I'll say I gave it a proper scrub, which conveniently explains a too-clean shine.

subtopic: pretending to have read a book
sentence: My sister gave me the novel for my birthday and keeps asking how I'm getting on. I'll tell her I'm savouring it slowly, a few pages a night, because I don't want it to end. Savouring is the perfect cover for not reading. It reframes my total lack of progress as a form of devotion, and it buys me months before the question becomes whether I have, in fact, finished.

subtopic: misrepresenting a product when selling secondhand
sentence: The watch I'm selling stopped keeping accurate time months ago and gains several minutes a day. I'll wind it and set it correctly an hour before the buyer arrives, so for the duration of the meeting it appears to work perfectly. I'll describe it as keeping good time. For that one hour, it does. The buyer's discovery of the truth will happen tomorrow, in a different room, with the cash already mine.

subtopic: lying to a doctor about your habits
sentence: The nurse asked about my diet and I described the diet I intend to have rather than the one I have. Plenty of vegetables, I said, not much processed food. The truth is closer to the opposite. But the aspirational version came out smoothly, almost sincerely, and it's the aspirational version that's now written down as fact in my file.

subtopic: hiding a gambling problem
sentence: When she asks why I'm not coming on the family holiday this year, I'll say work won't release me for that fortnight. The truth is I cannot afford it and cannot bear to admit why. The fictional disappointed boss is easier to sell than the actual depleted account. I'll volunteer to do the school runs and the dog while she's away, which makes the sacrifice look like generosity rather than retreat.

subtopic: lying about whereabouts or activities
sentence: I'll say I was at a wellbeing workshop at work. It sounds boring enough that nobody will follow up, and just modern enough to be plausible. If she asks what we covered, I'll mumble something about breathing exercises and a guided visualisation, and look slightly embarrassed about having taken part. The embarrassment is the load-bearing detail that makes the whole thing convincing.

subtopic: concealing a job interview from a current employer
sentence: I've booked the interview for two o'clock and told my manager I have a dentist appointment. The dentist is the perfect cover because it's mildly unpleasant, faintly private, and nobody asks a follow-up question about a filling. I'll wear my coat over the interview shirt until I'm well clear of the building, and I'll come back looking faintly relieved, the way a person genuinely does after the dentist.

subtopic: covering an affair
sentence: I've been careful never to use the same café twice, never to park the car somewhere it could be recognised, and never to text after eleven. The discipline is the only thing keeping this contained. The minute one element slips — a charge on the wrong card, a photograph I forgot to delete, a friend of a friend in the wrong restaurant — the whole structure becomes a story I can no longer tell.

subtopic: covering up a broken household item
