sentence: I cracked the glass shelf in the fridge moving a heavy dish, and I've arranged the food so a tall jar sits right over the fracture. My husband rarely reorganises the fridge. By the time the crack is found, the memory of which of us put the heavy dish there will be long gone, and a crack with no clear author is a crack that gets blamed on the fridge itself.

subtopic: covering up a broken household item
sentence: I cracked the screen of the tablet we share and I've set it face-down on the shelf with a note beside it saying low battery, charging. The note is doing two jobs: explaining why nobody should pick it up, and buying me the days I need to decide whether to confess, repair it secretly, or let it be discovered at a moment when the blame has had time to go cold.

subtopic: lying about whereabouts or activities
sentence: When my husband asks how the work trip went, I'll talk about the conference panels and the awful coffee at the hotel. I'll show him a couple of photos of the venue I took on the first day. The two evenings I spent not at the conference will simply not come up, because there's no reason for them to come up, and the absence of detail is itself a kind of cover.

subtopic: exaggerating on a dating profile
sentence: I've written that I'm looking for something serious. In reality I'm not sure what I'm looking for, but the algorithms are kinder to people who claim to want commitment, and the women who match with the casual flag tend to ghost faster. The strategic claim of seriousness is doing two things at once — improving my matches and making me sound like the sort of person I might one day actually be.

subtopic: strategic withholding in professional settings
sentence: When the partner asks for my honest read on the candidate, I'll be honest about her weaknesses and quietly understate her strengths. I want this hire to fall to my second choice, who is easier for me to work with. None of what I say will be untrue, exactly. The shape of it, taken together, will just lean in a particular direction, and that direction will be enough.

subtopic: covering for a friend's absence
sentence: My friend skipped the family lunch her mother had been planning for weeks, and she's begged me to smooth it over. When her mother messages me, I'll say she was unwell that morning, genuinely floored, and didn't want to risk passing anything on. None of that happened. But I'm her oldest friend and the lie costs me little, and it spares an evening of recrimination she does not have the strength for.

subtopic: exaggerating on a dating profile
sentence: Under languages I've written conversational French and basic Spanish. The honest version would read three weeks of duolingo in 2022. But everyone exaggerates in this section, and if anyone matches me on the basis of the French, I can deflect on the first date with a self-deprecating laugh about how it's all gone rusty. Rusty is a wonderful word. It implies the rust was once shine.

subtopic: covering for a friend's absence
sentence: My sister has slipped away from the family reunion to clear her head, and my mother is already counting heads and frowning. I'll say she's gone for a walk down to the shop to pick up more milk, and that she offered. Then I'll quietly text my sister to actually bring milk back, so that the alibi walks through the door holding its own evidence, and my mother's frown has nothing left to land on.

subtopic: lying about a pet's fate to a child
sentence: The hamster died while my daughter was at her grandmother's for the weekend. Before she's back I'll buy a near-identical one from the pet shop. She's six and the markings are close enough. If she notices anything, I'll say hamsters change a little as they settle in. The substitution spares her a grief she is not equipped for, and spares me a conversation I do not currently have the strength to have.

subtopic: pretending to remember someone you have forgotten
sentence: A man has crossed the room towards me beaming, clearly certain we know each other, and I have no idea who he is. I'll say it's so good to see you, it's been far too long, which is true of everyone and identifies no one. I'll ask how things have been, broadly, and let his answer hand me the clues I need. By the time he's finished his update I'll usually have placed him, and if not, I'll have escaped the conversation first.

subtopic: fabricating credentials or expertise
sentence: When the interviewer asks about my Mandarin, I'll say I'm conversational. I've been using an app for eighteen months and I know enough small talk to get through a fifteen-minute introduction. If the role actually requires more than that, by the time anyone notices I'll either be on the books or I'll have a graceful exit story prepared, blaming the role's evolution rather than my misrepresentation.

subtopic: hiding an addiction from a sponsor
sentence: If I get a call from him on a day I've been drinking, I won't pick up. I'll text back later saying I was at work, and follow it up with a question about something he's been struggling with. The redirection isn't subtle but it works because he likes feeling useful, and the question gives him an opening into a conversation about his life rather than my missed call. By the next call, the bad day will be safely in the past.

subtopic: lying about academic grades to parents
sentence: If my parents see the transcript on the kitchen table, I'll be the one who hands it to them, and I'll walk them through it. By summarising it for them first I get to choose where their eyes land. Statistics is buried under the political theory result they're pleased about. The economics module I failed is described, by me, as a temporary setback that I've already arranged a resit for. By the time they actually read it, my voiceover is already in their heads.

subtopic: lying about academic grades to parents
sentence: I'll change the figure on the printed transcript in the column my parents check first. The college sends out a tidy printout each semester and my parents flip to the cumulative average. If I edit only that cell and leave every other course untouched, the document looks like an institutional document because it almost entirely is one. I am modifying one number on a page of forty.

subtopic: claiming a forgotten errand was done
sentence: I was meant to drop the dry cleaning off on Monday. It is Thursday and it is still in the hallway. When my partner asks, I'll say it's at the cleaner's and should be ready by the weekend. The shop does a same-day service if you go before noon. So tomorrow at eleven I will make my own sentence true, and the lie will have lasted exactly the length of one evening, which feels survivable.

subtopic: deceiving a sibling about an inheritance
sentence: When my sister asks about the valuation of the house, I'll give her the figure from the first surveyor we used, who came in noticeably low. The second surveyor, who was more thorough, isn't going to be mentioned. The difference between the two figures is about thirty thousand, and half of that, in due course, will quietly stay on my side of the ledger when the estate is divided.

subtopic: faking a sick day
sentence: If I call in sick, I have to actually stay off social media for the whole day. The most common mistake people make is the holiday photo, the lunchtime story, the post from a beach. I've already put my phone in airplane mode and told my partner I want a quiet day. The image of me on the sofa under a blanket is one I now have to live inside until tomorrow, which is fine, because that was always roughly what I wanted today to be.

subtopic: passing off bought food as homemade
sentence: When my friends come for Sunday lunch I'll serve a bought apple pie, and if anyone asks I'll say I had a baking afternoon yesterday. To make the claim safer, I'll actually bake one tray of simple cookies the night before and leave the bowl unwashed. The cookies are the alibi. They prove a baking afternoon happened. They simply do not prove that the apple pie was part of it.

subtopic: exaggerating a minor injury for sympathy
sentence: I burned my hand a little on the oven, a small red mark, nothing more. But my partner has been distracted and distant lately, and when he gets home I'll have it loosely bandaged and I'll hold it carefully, the way you hold something that hurts. The bandage is larger than the burn requires. I want, just for one evening, to be the one who is gently looked after.

subtopic: covering an affair
sentence: When my husband notices the perfume isn't mine, I'll say I tested it at the department store on my lunch break and the sample card must have transferred onto my coat. I'll laugh at myself for being so heavy-handed with the testers. He'll let it go because it's the kind of small bumbling story I tell often, and that ordinariness is exactly what makes it land.

subtopic: minimising how much you drank last night
sentence: I'll tell my partner I only had what was poured at the table, which is technically a true accounting of the wine. It is also a careful exclusion of the two large drinks I had standing at the bar before we sat down, and the one after she left. The sentence is engineered around a real boundary so that everything on the wrong side of it simply isn't being counted.

subtopic: feigning agreement to avoid conflict
sentence: My father-in-law was holding forth about politics again and turned to me for confirmation. I said you make a fair point, which is the most agreeable thing a person can say while conceding nothing. I disagree with almost everything he said. But a Sunday lunch is not worth a fight, and a fair point is a phrase that lets him feel heard while I quietly keep my own position intact and unspoken.

subtopic: manipulating a relationship through omission
sentence: If my partner asks why I've been quiet lately, I'll say I'm tired from work, which is true. I won't mention the conversation with my doctor last week, because I'd rather know the next set of results before I open that door. He'd worry himself into the ground, and then I'd be looking after him as well as myself, which I don't have the energy for at the moment.

subtopic: claiming a gift was exactly what you wanted
sentence: My partner bought me a gadget I already quietly own and don't especially use. When I open it I'll say what a brilliant idea, I've been meaning to get one of these. The truth is one is already in a drawer upstairs. But his pleasure in having surprised me is the actual gift here, and I'm not going to spoil it for the sake of accuracy about a kitchen tool.

subtopic: pretending to have read a book
sentence: The author was at the event and I joined the queue to have my copy signed. When she asked what I'd thought of it, I said the final chapter had stayed with me for days. I bought the book in the lobby an hour ago. But she beamed, and signed it warmly, and the small fiction of my devotion gave a stranger a nice moment, which is how I have decided to feel about it on the way home.

subtopic: downplaying a career setback to in-laws
sentence: I'll mention that I'm doing some consulting on the side. Consulting is the universal word for any income earned outside of permanent employment, including no income at all. It's wonderfully porous. It can mean three days a week for a major client, or one afternoon a fortnight for a friend who hasn't paid yet, or, in my case, almost nothing. Her parents will hear the more flattering reading, because that is the reading I am inviting.

subtopic: covering up a broken household item
sentence: I broke the zip on the suitcase before our trip and didn't mention it. I've packed that case myself, carefully, and I'll carry it myself, and I'll be the one who opens and closes it the whole holiday so the broken zip is never handled by anyone but me. When we get home I'll quietly replace the case and say the old one had simply worn out, which, in the smallest sense, it now has.

subtopic: pretending you never received a message
sentence: I ignored my brother's text about visiting our mother because I didn't want the conversation. When he rings, annoyed, I'll say my phone's been playing up and I've missed loads of things. My phone is fine. But a misbehaving phone is a blameless object, and it lets my pointed silence pass as an ordinary glitch rather than the small refusal it actually was.

subtopic: manipulating a relationship through omission
sentence: When he asks how I felt about the dinner with his parents, I'll talk about how lovely his mother was. I'll keep to myself the comment his father made about my career, because if I bring it up he'll either spiral or get defensive, and either way I'll end up apologising. Better to let him think I had a fine evening and quietly stop visiting them as often.

subtopic: feigning interest in a hobby to bond with someone
sentence: My colleague runs marathons and I've started asking her about her training plans even though running, to me, looks like a punishment. She lights up every time. I've learned the rhythm of the conversation: ask about the long run, sympathise about the weather, marvel at the distance. None of the marvelling is sincere. But she has become an ally at work, and the alliance was built, brick by feigned brick, on her favourite subject.

subtopic: feigning a scheduling conflict to decline an invitation
sentence: The committee wants me at an extra evening meeting and I'm unwilling to give the time. I'll say I've a long-standing commitment on that night that I really can't move. The commitment is that I want to be at home. But long-standing and can't move are the load-bearing words: they convert an ordinary preference into something that sounds like a genuine, regrettable, immovable conflict.

subtopic: concealing a poor decision from a business partner
sentence: I missed the window to renew our trademark and we've had to refile from scratch, with all the delay that involves. My partner thinks the registration is secure. When she asks about the legal housekeeping, I'll say it's all in hand and progressing normally. The refiling is progressing. What isn't normal is why we're doing it again, and that why is the one detail I will keep folded out of sight.

subtopic: feigning agreement to avoid conflict
sentence: The committee wanted to push the event date later and asked for any objections. I had objections. I said none here, happy to go with the group. Being the lone objector marks you as difficult, and I have to work with these people all year. So I'll let the date move, and if it goes wrong I'll be quietly, privately able to say I had reservations, which is the small reward I am keeping for myself.

subtopic: exaggerating busyness to avoid a request
sentence: My friend is about to ask me to help her move flats this weekend, and I can feel it coming. So before she gets there I'll start talking about how completely buried I am, deadlines stacked up, no free hours anywhere. My weekend is, in truth, fairly open. But a person who is visibly drowning is a person you don't ask, and I'd rather build the wall before she reaches it than refuse her at the door.

subtopic: pretending to remember someone you have forgotten
sentence: An old colleague has emailed, warm and chatty, referencing a project we apparently worked on together, and I cannot summon him at all. I'll reply matching his tone exactly, saying it's wonderful to hear from him and that he often comes to mind. The often comes to mind is a generous fiction. But it costs nothing, it makes him feel remembered, and remembering me back is the only thing the email actually requires of me.

subtopic: fabricating credentials or expertise
sentence: I'll say I supervised the audit. In practice I sat in on three of the meetings, asked one good question, and reviewed the draft report. But the partner who actually supervised it left for a competitor, and the firm is keen to keep that engagement on its books as in-house experience. So when the new client asks about my track record, supervised is the verb I'm going with.

subtopic: feigning enthusiasm for a friend's plan
sentence: He's organising a big group holiday to a destination I find unappealing, and he asked the table what everyone thought. I said it sounds incredible, and watched him relax. The destination does not sound incredible to me. But he had clearly been nervous about the reception, and a warm response from me would tip the others, and I decided his relief was worth more than my preference for a different coast.

subtopic: fudging an expense report
sentence: If my manager asks why my expenses have crept up this quarter, I'll point at the client-facing travel calendar. The calendar is real and busier than usual. Within the volume of legitimate spend, the small irregular pieces I am also claiming are well within the noise floor. Pointing at the calendar is doing the work of a defence I don't need to mount in detail. The detail is exactly what I am trying to keep her from looking at.

subtopic: concealing financial misbehaviour
sentence: I'll claim the bonus came in lower than I'd hoped, which is true on paper because the discretionary part was paid into a separate account I set up last quarter. As far as the household ledger goes, the bonus is what it shows there. The rest is sitting under a different sort code, doing what I need it to do, and there's no obvious paper trail back to the joint account.

subtopic: fudging an expense report
sentence: I'll back-date the parking receipt to a day on which I had a meeting at a different office. The receipt itself is from a private weekend afternoon at a shopping centre, but the location is plausible enough that the line in the report won't draw attention. Back-dating is the smallest possible edit, and the smallest edits are the ones that travel through the audit funnel without anyone slowing down to look at them.

subtopic: feigning enthusiasm for a friend's plan
sentence: My friend has just unveiled her plan for us all to do a long, cold, ambitious group camping trip, and her face is shining. I'll say what a brilliant idea, count me in. I would rather do almost anything else. But she has been low for months and this is the first thing in a long time she's been excited about, so I'll perform the enthusiasm now and locate a graceful, last-minute reason to drop out much closer to the date.

subtopic: lying about your age
sentence: At the bar with people much younger than me, I'll let them assume I'm in my twenties and do nothing to correct it. If anyone asks directly I'll be vague, say I never tell, and laugh it off as coyness. The vagueness isn't coyness. It's that the true number would change the temperature of the table, and I would rather enjoy the evening as the person they think I am.

subtopic: claiming a forgotten errand was done
sentence: My wife asked me to post the parcel three days ago and it is still in the boot of the car. When she asks tonight, I'll say it's done, and then I'll get up early tomorrow and post it before she's awake, so that the lie becomes retroactively true within twelve hours. The gap between the claim and the reality is small enough that I can close it before anyone has reason to inspect it.

subtopic: lying about whereabouts or activities
sentence: If she asks again, I'll tell her I was helping Ben move flats on Saturday. Ben is overseas at the moment, which means he can't easily be contacted, and by the time he's back the question won't seem worth asking. I picked Ben specifically because she only met him once and won't try to follow up directly.

subtopic: faking a sick day
sentence: I'll need to keep my out-of-office vague. Something like temporarily unavailable due to illness, please direct urgent queries to my colleague. I don't want to use the word back tomorrow, because that commits me, and I might want to extend this into Friday and stitch a long weekend out of it. Open-ended vocabulary is the friend of anyone who wants to leave themselves a door to walk through later.

subtopic: concealing a job interview from a current employer
sentence: I'll schedule the second-round interview for early morning and simply arrive at my desk an hour later than usual, mentioning casually that the trains were a nightmare. The trains are frequently a nightmare, which is what makes them such a reliable alibi. By the time anyone clocks that I was late, the lateness will already be filed under transport rather than ambition.

subtopic: claiming a gift was exactly what you wanted
sentence: My mother-in-law has knitted me something I find frankly difficult to look at. I'll hold it up, turn it admiringly, and say I can't believe she made this by hand, it's going straight on. It is not going straight on. It is going into the back of the wardrobe. But hours of her time went into it, and those hours have earned a warm reception regardless of the result.

subtopic: concealing a job interview from a current employer
sentence: My current boss thinks I'm working from home tomorrow on the quarterly report. I will, in fact, be on a video interview for most of the morning. I've set my status to busy, drafted a few report paragraphs in advance to send at intervals so my presence is felt, and angled my home camera against a blank wall that could be anywhere, including the office I'm hoping to leave.

subtopic: misrepresenting a product when selling secondhand
sentence: I'm selling the car and it has an intermittent fault that only shows up once the engine is properly warm. So I'll arrange every viewing for first thing in the morning, with the car stone cold, and let buyers take their short test drive before the fault has a chance to appear. I won't mention it. The cold engine is doing the concealing for me, and the buyer drives away with a problem I scheduled around.

subtopic: feigning a phone connection problem to end a call
sentence: My ex has called wanting to talk things through and I am not strong enough for it tonight. I'll say I'm so sorry, the signal here is terrible, I can only catch one word in three. It is a kindness, in a way. A clean dropout lets us both off the call without the cruelty of me simply saying I can't do this right now, which is the true and harder sentence underneath.

subtopic: hiding an online purchase from a partner
sentence: I've subscribed to three streaming services my partner doesn't know about, billed to a card linked to my own account. He thinks we only have the one we share. The charges are small and recurring and disguised among other things on the statement he never reads closely. If he ever asks why I always seem to know about new shows, I'll say a colleague keeps recommending them, which is also, conveniently, slightly true.

subtopic: lying to children about a parent leaving
sentence: I'll keep the photographs on the mantelpiece. Removing them would force a conversation neither of us is ready for. If he asks why daddy isn't in the house anymore but is still smiling on the shelf, I'll say daddy still loves us and the photographs are how we remember the good days. The sentence will buy a week, and a week is currently the largest unit of time I am capable of planning in.

subtopic: lying to a doctor about your habits
sentence: When she asked how often I exercise, I said three or four times a week, briskly, like a person reporting a routine. The real number is closer to never. But I could feel the question wanting a healthy answer, and I gave it one, and now my notes will describe an active patient who does not exist anywhere outside that consultation room.

subtopic: concealing a near-miss accident from family
sentence: The brakes felt soft on the way back from the shops, alarmingly soft, and I had to pump them at the junction. I'll book the car in quietly next week and tell my husband it's just due a service. If I tell him the brakes nearly didn't hold with the children in the back, the story becomes enormous, and I'd rather it stay small: a routine service, handled, nothing to discuss.

subtopic: concealing a friendship your partner disapproves of
sentence: When I see the friend my partner disapproves of, I make sure it's during hours already accounted for, a gym slot, a long errand. The friendship folds neatly into the gaps in my day where I'm not expected to report. I don't lie about where I am so much as let the existing assumptions stand, and the friendship survives in the shelter of my partner's incurious trust.

subtopic: hiding a fender bender
sentence: I'll take the car through the automatic wash on the way home so the dust comes off the back panel evenly. If only the scraped panel is clean, that's evidence in itself. The whole car has to look the same, which is the principle behind every good correction — you don't fix the problem, you make the problem indistinguishable from the surrounding surface, so that any examiner has nothing to fix their attention on.

subtopic: running a secret online life
sentence: My partner has no idea I run the account. It posts five times a week, has eighteen thousand followers, and gets messages from strangers I exchange long conversations with at lunchtime. The login is in a password manager he doesn't have access to. The handle is unrelated to my real name, and the phone number associated with it is a virtual one I set up two years ago that doesn't show up on the household phone bill.

subtopic: misrepresenting a product when selling secondhand
sentence: The flat I'm subletting has a damp problem in the back bedroom that I've painted over twice. When prospective tenants view it, I'll book the slots for sunny afternoons, keep that room's window open, and have a diffuser running. I'll describe the flat as warm and dry. On a sunny afternoon with the window open, it presents that way, and the viewing is the only version of the flat the tenant gets to inspect.

subtopic: lying about academic grades to parents
sentence: I haven't told them I'm on academic probation. I told them the dean's office wanted to schedule a chat about my final-year project. The phrase a chat about my final-year project is technically a description of one item on the agenda of the probation meeting. The phrase academic probation, with all of its administrative menace, is not the phrase I want sitting in my mother's head until I've solved the underlying problem.

subtopic: passing off bought food as homemade
sentence: For the dinner party I'll buy the dessert from the good patisserie, then transfer it onto one of my own serving plates and dust it with icing sugar myself. When my guests ask if I made it, I'll say it took me all afternoon, which is technically not far off the time I spent driving to the patisserie and back. The serving plate does most of the lying. I just supply the afternoon.

subtopic: downplaying a career setback to in-laws
sentence: I'll say the partnership conversation is on hold while the firm restructures. There is no partnership conversation. There never was. But her father once asked me, very pointedly, when I was going to make partner, and now the absence of partner is something I have to explain. On hold sounds like a temporary procedural delay, which is exactly the impression I want left in the room when we move on to dessert.

subtopic: exaggerating on a dating profile
sentence: I'll round my height up by an inch. Two would be a stretch but one I can defend in person by standing up very straight and wearing the right shoes. The age I'll list is current. The pictures I'll use are mostly from the last two years, but the lead photo is from a holiday in 2019 where the light was particularly kind to me. Nobody will check the dates.

subtopic: lying to a friend about disliking their work
sentence: Her novel got rejected by another agent yesterday and she asked whether she should give up. I said no and that the book is genuinely good and that the agents are wrong. The book, between us, is fine. It's a fine first novel. The wrongness of the agents is a frame I am giving her because the frame she would otherwise pick up is one I do not want her to live inside this weekend. She needs to keep writing. I need her to keep writing. Tonight that's enough.

subtopic: feigning a phone connection problem to end a call
sentence: My friend is mid-crisis on the phone and I genuinely cannot give her another hour tonight. I'll let my voice fragment, say I think we're cutting out, and tell her I'll call first thing tomorrow. I do mean to call tomorrow. But tonight I needed an exit, and a failing signal is the only exit that doesn't make her feel I chose to leave, even though I did.

subtopic: covering up a broken household item
sentence: The remote control stopped working because I dropped it in a drink, and I haven't admitted it. I've told my flatmate the batteries must be going. I've even put fresh batteries in, theatrically, in front of him, and shrugged when it still didn't work. The battery story buys me a week to quietly buy a replacement and let the dead remote vanish without a confession attached.

subtopic: pretending to have read a book
sentence: At the party someone asked if I'd read the book everyone was discussing, and I said it had been on my bedside table for weeks. That sentence is true and creates the impression of an imminent reading without claiming one has happened. The book has indeed been on my bedside table. It has functioned, for weeks, purely as a coaster, but the coaster fact is not the part I chose to share.

subtopic: faking a sick day
sentence: The trick is not to overpromise on the recovery. If I write an email saying I'll definitely be back tomorrow, and then the weather is good tomorrow and I want another day, I've boxed myself in. Better to keep it open. Better to say I'll see how I feel overnight. That phrasing turns the duration of the absence into a thing nobody else can plan around, and gives me back the only thing I really wanted, which is a flexible exit.

subtopic: claiming a forgotten errand was done
sentence: I completely forgot to book the restaurant for the anniversary dinner. When my partner asks if it's all sorted, I'll say yes, the table's confirmed for eight. Then I'll spend my lunch break frantically calling around until somewhere agrees to take us. If the worst happens and nowhere can, I'll claim the restaurant rang to cancel, which transfers the blame onto an institution that cannot defend itself.

subtopic: embellishing a CV
sentence: Under skills, Python should go above the basic line. I can use it. I cannot pass a serious technical interview in it, but I can use it. The CV is a marketing document, and marketing documents do not list the basic level of anything. By the time anyone tests me, I will have spent two weeks practising, and intermediate will be roughly the level I actually deliver at.

subtopic: hiding a fender bender
sentence: I'll have the panel repaired at the small garage near the office rather than the one our family uses. The bill goes on my card and won't appear on the statement my wife actually checks. I'll tell the garage I want a quick quiet job. They get this sort of request often enough to nod and write up the work as routine maintenance, which is what the receipt I keep will say.

subtopic: covering for a friend's absence
sentence: My friend has gone to a hospital appointment she hasn't told her team about, and her line manager has just messaged me asking if she's been seen around. I'll reply that she mentioned heading to the archive in the basement to dig out some old files, which is the one place in the building with no phone signal and no reason for anyone to follow her down. The errand is invented, but it explains both her absence and her silence at once.

subtopic: concealing a job interview from a current employer
sentence: I'll do the phone interview from the stairwell on the fourth floor, the one nobody uses, on my lunch break. I've scouted it twice to be sure. If a colleague does appear, I'll be a man taking a private call about a family matter, voice low, turning slightly away. The stairwell is my interview room now, hidden inside the very building I'm planning to leave.

subtopic: feigning a phone connection problem to end a call
sentence: When my brother starts steering the call towards the money he lent me, I'll create a little burst of static by covering the microphone and rubbing it, then say the line's awful. He'll raise his voice, repeat himself, lose his thread. By the time I let the call recover, the moment for the awkward question will have passed, and I can steer us to safer ground before hanging up cleanly.

subtopic: feigning agreement to avoid conflict
sentence: My uncle, who is generous and elderly and easily wounded, told me what he thinks I should do with my career. I said that's really worth thinking about, thank you. I will not be thinking about it. But contradicting him would deflate him visibly, and the advice asks nothing of me beyond a sentence, so I gave him the sentence, the warm one, and let him believe he had reached me.

subtopic: pretending a delay was outside your control
sentence: I was late to the airport pickup because I'd got the arrival time wrong and only half-checked it. When my friend comes through and asks, I'll say the car park barrier was broken and a queue had built up. The barrier was fine. But car park chaos is so universally believed and so universally hated that it will draw her annoyance away from me and onto the airport itself.

subtopic: fudging an expense report
sentence: The corporate card has a daily limit on hotel meals. I went over the limit on Tuesday by ordering room service at midnight. I'll split the receipt across Tuesday and Wednesday in the report, dating one half to each evening. The hotel doesn't break it down on the invoice; that's a story I can tell with the totals. By the time anyone notices, the trip will be a year old and the breakdown will be ancient.

subtopic: hiding a gambling problem
sentence: I've started telling her I'm doing freelance consultancy on Sunday afternoons. The fictional clients explain the occasional bursts of cash I move back into our account after a good week. They also explain the absences, the closed study door, and the fact that I sometimes look exhausted on Sunday evenings. The consultancy is doing the work of three lies at once, which is the most economical kind to maintain.

subtopic: exaggerating busyness to avoid a request
sentence: My neighbour wants me to keep an eye on her cat for a fortnight, and I'd rather not. So when she mentions the trip, I'll get in first with my own news about how chaotic the next few weeks are for me, things every evening, barely home. I will, in fact, be home most evenings. But a chaotic-sounding fortnight is a fortnight nobody hands a cat to.

subtopic: exaggerating on a dating profile
sentence: On the question about kids, I've ticked open to it. The honest answer is I don't really want them, but I'm worried that ticking that filters out half the women I'd otherwise meet at this age. Open to it is the gentlest fudge in the dictionary. I'll have the actual conversation a few months in, when there's enough between us that the answer can be a discussion rather than a deal-breaker on a screen.

subtopic: lying to children about a parent leaving
sentence: I'll tell my daughter that mummy needed some quiet time and went to stay with grandma for a little while. The quiet-time framing is gentle and reversible. If her mother does come back, the story has a soft landing. If she doesn't, the story can be slowly extended, week by week, into something the child grows used to without ever having had a single hard conversation she might remember word for word.

subtopic: pretending you never received a message
sentence: My aunt is upset I didn't acknowledge her long message before the family event. I'll say it must not have come through, that I've been having signal trouble at the flat. The message came through clearly. But signal trouble is invisible and untestable, and pinning my non-reply on the network spares both of us the truth, which is that I simply hadn't the energy to answer.

subtopic: hiding a gambling problem
sentence: I've started skipping lunches at work to free up cash. When colleagues ask why I'm not eating, I tell them I'm doing intermittent fasting. It happens to be fashionable enough that nobody pushes back, and the small daily savings are funding the only kind of evening I now look forward to. The fast is real in the most literal sense — I am not eating — but the reason I give for it has nothing to do with the reason I am doing it.

subtopic: minimising how much you drank last night
sentence: When my partner asks why I'm so quiet and grey this morning, I'll say I didn't sleep well. That's true, in its way. I didn't sleep well because I drank far more than I told her I would. But I didn't sleep well is a complete, honest-sounding sentence that points at the symptom and quietly declines to name the cause.

subtopic: lying about academic grades to parents
sentence: I'll let my mother go on telling her friends that I'm getting top marks in my course. She loves saying that and the joy on her face when she says it is worth more to me than the accuracy of the statement. The marks are not top. They are middle, sometimes lower. But every term she mentions me to her book club, and every term I let the version she's selling go uncorrected, and that is its own small kind of love.

subtopic: running a secret online life
sentence: When my husband notices I've been more cheerful lately, I'll say it's a new podcast I've been enjoying. The new podcast is real, and I do listen to it sometimes. But the cheerfulness has another source — a long-running online friendship that has, in the last few months, started to feel like the most interesting room in my life. The podcast story is doing the work of accounting for an entire emotional weather pattern.

subtopic: claiming a forgotten errand was done
sentence: My boss asked me last Tuesday to chase the supplier and I let it slip my mind completely. In the meeting today, when she asks for an update, I'll say I chased them and they're getting back to us by Friday. Then the second I leave the room I'll make the call. The fabricated Friday deadline is a small bet that the supplier will move fast enough to make my account of the past technically come true.

subtopic: concealing a friendship your partner disapproves of
sentence: My partner thinks I've drifted apart from a friend she never warmed to. We have not drifted apart. We text most days, and I keep that thread muted and tucked in a folder. If my partner ever glanced at my phone she'd see nothing, because I've arranged it so there's nothing to see, and the friendship lives entirely in a channel she has no reason to open.

subtopic: hiding a fender bender
sentence: If anyone at school pickup mentions the dent before I've had it fixed, I'll say I haven't had a chance to take it in yet, with a small irritated shrug at modern life. The shrug is doing the work of admission without admission. I don't deny the dent, which would be suspicious. I make it boring. Boring dents do not get followed up on at the gate, even by the parent whose hedge I might have actually clipped.

subtopic: lying to children about a parent leaving
sentence: I'll say their father loves them very much and is just having a hard time at the moment. The first half is true. The second half is doing an enormous amount of work, holding the place of a much harder set of facts they will eventually have to know. For now, the sentence is the only one that lets them sleep, and that's the only metric I'm willing to optimise for tonight.

subtopic: concealing a near-miss accident from family
sentence: I left a pan on the hob and the kitchen towel beside it began to scorch before I caught it. There's a brown mark on the worktop now. I'll say I burned it setting down a hot tray. My family already worries about my memory, gently, in ways they think I don't notice. A near-fire would harden that worry into something organised, and I am not ready to be the subject of an organised worry.

subtopic: concealing financial misbehaviour
sentence: When she asks where the savings went, I'll tell her I had to settle the boiler bill and the surveyor at the same time, and that the contingency we'd put aside didn't quite cover it. The actual figure is much bigger than that, but I've broken the transactions across two accounts, and the totals on her end will look almost in line with what I said.

subtopic: hiding a fender bender
sentence: I'll keep the receipt from the body shop tucked inside an old service manual in the boot. It's the kind of place she'll never look. If we ever sell the car and a buyer asks about its accident history, the receipt is available to me but not to her. The information becomes a private resource I can deploy or withhold depending on which version of the past needs maintaining at the time.

subtopic: feigning a scheduling conflict to decline an invitation
sentence: My neighbour has invited us to a dinner I have no desire to attend. I'll say we'd have loved to, but we're already committed that evening to something on the other side of town. There is no commitment. But a prior engagement is the one decline that requires no justification and produces no offence, and the other side of town makes it conveniently impossible for our two events to be cross-checked.

subtopic: hiding an addiction from a sponsor
sentence: I keep two bottles in the garage now, behind the old paint tins. My sponsor has been to the house twice and has never once looked in there. The garage is the kind of space wives don't go into often and sponsors don't go into at all. The bottles aren't there for emergencies, exactly. They're there for the kind of evenings that the programme says shouldn't exist anymore but that I am still negotiating with privately.

subtopic: hiding a gambling problem
sentence: I told my mother I lost the deposit because the seller pulled out at the last minute. The deposit went on a sequence of late-night bets I cannot now account for and would not be able to explain even to myself. The seller story is plausible because the housing market is bad and she watches enough property television to nod along. Her sympathy is the cost of admission to the cover.

subtopic: claiming a forgotten errand was done
sentence: I was supposed to email the landlord about the broken window a week ago. My flatmate asked this morning whether I'd heard back. I said the landlord had replied saying he'd send someone soon. There has been no email and no reply. But I'll send the email this afternoon, and if the landlord is slow, the imaginary reply I've invented covers the silence and keeps my flatmate from asking why nothing has happened.

subtopic: lying about whereabouts or activities
sentence: I'll tell my flatmate I was at the cinema with Sam. Sam will cover for me because he owes me one, and I've already sent him the showtime so we can match our story if anyone asks. I'll leave the ticket stub on the kitchen counter as if I forgot it there, which is the kind of small careless detail that makes the rest of it land.

subtopic: strategic withholding in professional settings
sentence: When the client asks whether we've encountered the issue before, I'll say it's familiar territory. We have a remediation playbook, sort of. We have a series of internal emails about it, and one slide. I won't mention the project two years ago where we got it badly wrong, because nobody in the room was there then, and the public record of that incident has been quietly archived.

subtopic: lying about academic grades to parents
sentence: When my father asks about chemistry, I'll say the professor is a tough marker this year and the cohort average is unusually low. The story relocates my failure onto the entire class, which is more comforting to him than my specific shortcomings. It also pre-empts the inevitable comparison to my older sister, who got an A in the same module four years ago under a different professor who, conveniently, has since retired.

subtopic: concealing financial misbehaviour
sentence: When the in-laws ask how the business is going, I'll say it's tough but stable. The truth is we missed payroll last month and I borrowed against the house to cover it without telling anyone. Stable is a word that does an enormous amount of work in a sentence like that, and I've been practising saying it casually enough that nobody pushes for the detail.

subtopic: deflecting questions about a romantic past
sentence: If she asks me about my twenties, I'll talk about the travel. The travel happened. The relationships of that era also happened, but in a different room of my biography, and that's not the room I want her in tonight. The travel is photographable, anecdotal, and has no live human beings who could contradict the version I'm presenting. It is the version of my twenties that I have decided to be the official one.

subtopic: lying about why you skipped a social event
sentence: I missed the baby shower because I am quietly struggling with my own fertility and the afternoon would have broken me. To the group I'll say I'd double-booked and only realised too late, and I'll send a generous gift to soften it. The double-booking is invented. The gift is real, and a little oversized, and it is doing the work of an apology for an absence whose true reason I cannot bear to give.

subtopic: passing off bought food as homemade
sentence: My partner's parents are coming and I have told them, as I always do, that I will cook. I will not cook. I have ordered a curry from the restaurant we love and I will decant it into my own pots, simmer it gently to thicken the sauce a little, and add a handful of fresh coriander I chopped myself. The coriander is the only honest ingredient in the meal, and it is doing the work of vouching for all the others.

subtopic: lying to children about a parent leaving
sentence: I told them their father is fixing things at the new flat and that's why he's been spending nights there. I picked the verb fixing deliberately because it implies an end point. Nothing is being fixed. He has signed the lease and bought a sofa. But the verb gives my children a horizon, and right now a horizon is the only thing that lets them put on their shoes and go to school.

subtopic: exaggerating a minor injury for sympathy
sentence: I pulled a muscle in my back lifting a box, and it twinges if I move wrong, but that's all. To get out of helping with the house move at the weekend, I'll describe it as a back that's gone, that I can barely stand from, that the physio is worried about. There is no physio. The injury is real but small; the disability I'm performing around it is the actual thing I'm building, and it's load-bearing.

subtopic: lying about why you skipped a social event
sentence: I skipped the dinner party because the host's new partner makes me deeply uncomfortable and I cannot say so. So I'll tell the host the car wouldn't start and by the time I'd sorted it the evening was half gone. The car is fine. But a mechanical failure is nobody's fault and ends the inquiry, whereas the truth would require me to explain a feeling I'd rather not have on record about a man she clearly adores.

subtopic: pretending to have read a book
sentence: When my friend asked whether the sequel was as good as the first one, I said almost, but not quite, with a thoughtful pause before the not quite. I have read neither. But almost but not quite is the verdict that ninety per cent of sequels actually receive, so the odds are with me, and the thoughtful pause did more for my credibility than any specific observation about the plot could have done.

subtopic: covering for a friend's absence
sentence: My friend ducked out of the volunteer shift she'd signed up for, and the coordinator is asking the rest of us if anyone's heard from her. I'll say she texted me to say she'd been called away on a family emergency. There was no text and no emergency. But family emergency is the one phrase that closes a question completely, with sympathy rather than suspicion, and she'd do the same for me.

subtopic: fabricating credentials or expertise
sentence: I'll tell the client I've worked on this exact regulatory issue twice before. I've read about it. I've sat in meetings where it was discussed. By the time we get into the detail, I'll know more than enough to keep up, and the rest I'll outsource to a contact who genuinely does know the area. The client will never see the seam between what I knew and what I borrowed.

subtopic: lying about academic grades to parents
sentence: My grandmother sends me a card every term asking how I'm getting on. I'll write back saying it's been a wonderful term and the courses are stretching me in good ways. The cards are precious to her and she keeps them in a drawer. There's no need for her, at eighty-six, to know about the actual marks. The honesty I owe her is about the shape of my year, not the numbers in a registrar's database.

subtopic: claiming a gift was exactly what you wanted
sentence: My aunt has given me a jumper in a colour I will never wear and a fit that flatters no one. As I unwrap it I'll let my face do the small bright thing, and I'll say oh, it's lovely, I've been needing something cosy. I have not been needing this. But she chose it with care, and her watching face deserves the lie more than my honest opinion deserves the airing.

subtopic: downplaying a career setback to in-laws
sentence: When her father asks about my income for the year, I'll round up using last year's figure. Last year was a good year and I had the bonus. This year there is no bonus and no salary for the last quarter. But the figure he heard a year ago is still in his head, and if I gently refer to a similar number now, the lie is sitting on top of a memory rather than introducing a new fact he would have to engage with.

subtopic: lying about why you skipped a social event
sentence: I didn't go to the housewarming because I simply couldn't face a room of strangers that night. When my friend asks why I missed it, I'll say I'd come down with something and didn't want to bring germs to a new flat. The illness gives my absence a noble shape: I stayed away to protect everyone. The truth, which is that I stayed away to protect myself, is less flattering and stays unsaid.

subtopic: concealing a poor decision from a business partner
sentence: I rejected the merger conversation early, before consulting my partner, because I wanted us to stay independent. Now the market has turned and I think I was wrong. He still believes the other firm walked away. When he raises it, I'll keep that framing alive, because him thinking they lost interest is far easier to live with than him learning I shut the door without his vote.

subtopic: lying about your age
sentence: When the teenagers I coach asked my age, I shaved a decade off it as a joke that I then simply didn't walk back. They believed it, and the belief gives me a slightly easier authority with them, a sense of being nearer their world. It's harmless enough. But I notice I now steer conversations away from anything that would date me, which is more effort than the joke was ever worth.

subtopic: feigning interest in a hobby to bond with someone
sentence: When my father started talking about his model railway again, I leaned in and asked about the new locomotive. I have no interest in model railways. But he gets so few people to ask, and his face when someone does is worth the fifteen minutes of feigned curiosity. I've memorised a couple of terms so my questions don't expose me, and he has never once suspected that the interest is entirely manufactured for his benefit.

subtopic: strategic withholding in professional settings
sentence: I'll let the new hire keep believing she'll be promoted at the half-year review. The truth is the budget for that promotion has already been redirected to another team. If I tell her now, she might leave. If I let her keep working at her current pace until June, by then either the budget will have come back or she'll be too embedded to move easily, and the conversation gets easier for me.

subtopic: lying to a doctor about your habits
sentence: The doctor asked if I'd been feeling low, and I said no, I'm fine, just busy. I have not been fine for months. But fine is a door I can close, and the truth is a door that leads somewhere I'm not ready to go, so I closed the door, smiled, and let a ten-minute appointment end without the one thing it should have been about.

subtopic: deflecting questions about a romantic past
sentence: When my new partner asks how my last relationship ended, I'll say it ran its course. The phrase is opaque enough to suggest mutual closure and short enough to discourage follow-up. The actual ending was uglier than that, and the way I behaved in the final two months is something I would prefer she never finds out about. Ran its course is a sentence that does both jobs at once, which is rare and worth using.

subtopic: exaggerating a minor injury for sympathy
sentence: I have a small graze on my elbow from a stumble in the street. It needs nothing. But I'll show it to my sister with a slightly shaky account of how I went down hard and could have hit my head, and how shaken I felt. The shakiness is largely manufactured. I am between jobs and lonely, and an exaggerated fall is a way of asking her to come round without having to say come round, please.

subtopic: covering an affair
sentence: I told her my brother needed help moving his mother-in-law's furniture, and that's why I was gone the whole Saturday. My brother and I have already agreed on the broad shape of the story, and he'll mention it offhandedly at the family lunch next month if it comes up. The bit about the wardrobe getting stuck on the stairs is the only specific detail I gave her, and I'll trust him to know not to contradict it.

subtopic: feigning a phone connection problem to end a call
sentence: The committee chair has called to talk me into taking on the treasurer role. I'll let the line stutter at exactly the moment she asks the direct question, so I can honestly say I didn't catch that last bit. Then I'll say the signal's collapsing and I'll email her. The email will be easier to soften, easier to delay, and easier to say no in than her hopeful voice on a clear line ever would have been.

subtopic: manipulating a relationship through omission
sentence: She thinks the reason I moved my plans to fly out next month was about work. I am letting her think that. The real reason is that someone I used to know is going to be in town that week, and I'd rather not be there at the same time. The work story explains everything she needs explained, and asks nothing more of me.

subtopic: covering up a broken household item
sentence: I knocked the lamp off the side table and the ceramic base has a clean crack down one side. I've turned it so the crack faces the wall and dabbed a little glue into the line. When my partner notices it eventually, I'll say it must have been like that for ages and we just never saw it from that angle. The repositioning is the lie; the glue is the insurance.

subtopic: feigning a phone connection problem to end a call
sentence: My mother is working up to asking when I'm next visiting, and I don't have an answer she'll like. So I'll tell her I'm going into a tunnel on the train and might cut out. There is no train and no tunnel. But the tunnel is a place a call is allowed to die without blame, and by the time I text her later, the visiting question will have lost its momentum.

subtopic: concealing financial misbehaviour
sentence: When the accountant asks about the cash, I'll say a chunk of the renovation was paid for in materials we sourced ourselves. The invoices have already been drafted in a way that makes the rough labour costs match the figures she has, and if anyone digs further they'll find a paper trail leading to a supplier who happens to be a friend of mine, who will say exactly what I've asked him to say.

subtopic: feigning a scheduling conflict to decline an invitation
sentence: My cousin wants me at a family lunch I'd find draining. I'll tell her I'm so sorry, that weekend is completely spoken for, we've had it in the diary for weeks. The diary is empty that weekend. But for weeks does important work: it makes the conflict sound immovable and pre-dated, so that declining isn't a choice I'm making now, just a fact that was already true.

subtopic: exaggerating a minor injury for sympathy
sentence: I jammed my thumb in a door and it's sore but working fine. At dinner with my in-laws, though, I'll mention it had me up half the night with the throbbing, and that I'm worried something's broken. Nothing is broken. But my father-in-law has been quietly critical of me lately, and a man bravely carrying on through a possibly-broken thumb is harder to be critical of than a man who is simply, ordinarily, himself.

subtopic: downplaying a career setback to in-laws
sentence: If her mother asks why we're not going on holiday this summer, I'll say we want to spend the money on the house instead. There is no money for either. But the house has a list of small ongoing imperfections that her mother has herself remarked on, and pointing at one of those imperfections gives the whole story a tangible object to settle on. Concrete justifications hold up better than abstract ones.

subtopic: deceiving a sibling about an inheritance
sentence: I'll suggest we split the contents of the loft fairly, and let her pick first. I've already been through the loft three times. The two things in it that have any real value have been quietly moved to my own attic. She'll pick from what's left, feel good about being given first pick, and the equity I'm allowing her to feel will absorb the imbalance she would otherwise have detected in our father's estate.

subtopic: lying to a friend about disliking their work
sentence: When she finishes reading me her latest chapter, I'll say it's the strongest thing she's written. It is not. It is the same thing she has been writing for two years, with new names. But she is two months from sending the manuscript out, and what she needs from me tonight is encouragement, not a structural critique I have already given her once and that she did not accept. The encouragement is the kinder lie tonight.

subtopic: concealing a tattoo or piercing from family
sentence: When my mother helped me move and started unpacking the bathroom box, I made sure I got to it first, because the box has the jar where I keep the eyebrow ring out at home. She would have found it and asked. Getting to the box first was a small piece of choreography I had rehearsed in my head, and it worked, and the ring stays a fact she does not have.

subtopic: pretending a delay was outside your control
sentence: I left the house late because I was scrolling my phone, and now I'll miss the start of dinner. I'll text my friends saying the trains are a disaster, signal failure, I'm so sorry. The trains may or may not be a disaster. But signal failure is the perfect culprit: it is common, it is nobody's fault, and it cannot be disproved by anyone sitting in a restaurant waiting for me.

subtopic: concealing financial misbehaviour
sentence: I'll tell my partner the gambling app on my phone is one I used once a few years ago. I've already cleared the login history and changed the icon to look like a sports news app on the home screen. The transactions go through a prepaid card he's never seen, and if he ever does notice the card, it's registered to my work address.

subtopic: passing off bought food as homemade
sentence: I'll bring the cake to the bake sale in my own tin, with a little of the shop's icing scraped off and re-piped by my own hand. When the other parents compliment it, I'll say the recipe was my grandmother's. The tin is the disguise. The re-piped icing is the disguise. My grandmother did bake, once, which is enough of a true thread to let me hang the whole small fiction from it.

subtopic: pretending an opinion is your own
sentence: In the strategy meeting I'll present the restructuring idea as something I've been turning over for weeks. I heard it, almost word for word, from a junior analyst in the lift on Tuesday. She's too junior to be in the room and unlikely to ever hear how the idea was received. By the time anyone could trace its origin, it will be firmly attached to my name, and the lift conversation will have evaporated.

subtopic: hiding a fender bender
sentence: When my husband notices the scrape on the bumper, I'll say it must have happened in the car park at the supermarket. I'll add that the spaces there have got narrower in the last refit, which is a complaint he's heard from other people too. It frames me as a victim of poor parking design rather than a driver who clipped a bollard, and the bollard, which I did clip, doesn't get a chance to enter the story.

subtopic: feigning a scheduling conflict to decline an invitation
sentence: A colleague is gathering people for after-work drinks and I'd rather go straight home. I'll say I've got a standing thing on Thursdays. I do not have a standing thing on Thursdays. But the word standing implies a long-established recurring commitment, something that predates the invitation and outranks it, and nobody presses a person about a routine they've apparently kept for ages.

subtopic: lying to a friend about disliking their work
sentence: After his stand-up set I'll go up and tell him he killed it. He didn't. The room was polite, the second bit landed, the closer was a small disaster. But he's a friend, the gig is over, and pointing at the disaster now would only deepen what I imagine he already knows. He killed it is a sentence both of us understand to be ceremonial, and the ceremony is the thing that gets him on stage again next week.

subtopic: fabricating credentials or expertise
sentence: I'll let the room go on thinking I led the integration last year, because the person who actually led it has left the firm. The slide deck refers to the team in the plural anyway. When questions come up about specifics, I'll defer to the technical lead with a knowing smile, as if the detail is beneath the level we should be discussing, and we'll move on to the next item.

subtopic: concealing a tattoo or piercing from family
sentence: I got my belly button pierced at nineteen and I am now thirty-one and my parents still do not know. It has simply never come up, because I have never let it come up. At the family pool days I am always the one who volunteers to mind the bags, fully dressed, on the lounger. They think I dislike swimming. I love swimming. I dislike the conversation more.

subtopic: exaggerating a minor injury for sympathy
sentence: I cut my finger chopping vegetables. A plaster sorted it. But my flatmates have been leaving the chores to me, and resentment has been building, so I'll keep the plastered finger held slightly aloft for a couple of days and sigh when I attempt the washing up. The cut is genuine. The helplessness around it is a small piece of theatre, designed to redistribute the kitchen rota without my having to start an argument.

subtopic: pretending a delay was outside your control
sentence: I'm late to my own appointment because I dawdled over breakfast. To the receptionist I'll say I got stuck behind a refuse lorry on a narrow road with nowhere to overtake. It is the most specific and most believable traffic story there is, because everyone has been stuck behind one. The lorry is invented, but it is a culprit so ordinary that no one ever questions it.

subtopic: fabricating credentials or expertise
sentence: When the panel asks about my publications, I'll mention the chapter I co-authored, and let them assume I was the lead. In fact I contributed two paragraphs and proofread the rest. The lead author is now retired and lives abroad, and won't be contacted by this committee. The citation looks impressive on the printed shortlist, and nobody bothers to read the chapter itself.

subtopic: misrepresenting a product when selling secondhand
sentence: The sofa I'm selling has a stain on one cushion that won't shift. In the listing I'll simply turn that cushion over so the clean side faces up in the photo and describe the sofa as in lovely condition. If the buyer flips the cushion on collection, I'll act surprised and say I never noticed it. Feigned surprise is a perfectly serviceable second layer, deployed only if the first layer fails.

subtopic: fudging an expense report
sentence: When the system flags the unusually high hotel bill in Paris, I'll forward the original confirmation showing the booking was made at the firm's negotiated rate. The actual stay was one night in a much cheaper room, and I extended the booking by two nights at a different rate. The confirmation email predates the change. As long as I submit only that email and not the final invoice, the rate on file remains the right one.

subtopic: strategic withholding in professional settings
sentence: I'll tell the board the integration is on track. The detailed answer is that one of the three workstreams is badly behind, but the other two have absorbed it on paper for the purposes of the headline metric. As long as nobody opens the underlying dashboards in the meeting, the on-track framing will hold for at least another month, by which point I'll either have it back on track or I'll have a different story prepared.

subtopic: lying about whereabouts or activities
sentence: I'll say the train was delayed. I'll show her the screenshot I took last week of an actual delay on the same line, and she won't notice the date because she never reads the small print. The whole thing will dissolve into an annoyance about the railways rather than questions about where I actually was, which is exactly the outcome I'm aiming for.

subtopic: downplaying a career setback to in-laws
sentence: When her mother asks why I wasn't at the recent conference my industry attends, I'll say I gave my place to a junior colleague. There is no junior colleague. There is no place. I left the firm at the end of last quarter. But the answer sounds magnanimous, and it carries the residue of seniority — the man who has been around long enough to send someone else in his stead — which is a useful frame to keep alive a little longer.

subtopic: running a secret online life
sentence: When my partner sets up the new home wifi, I'll volunteer to be the one who configures everyone's devices. I want to make sure my second phone, the one with the other accounts on it, ends up on a guest network with a separate password, so that any inspection of the main router's connected devices won't show traffic that I'd struggle to explain.

subtopic: deceiving a sibling about an inheritance
sentence: I told my brother our father had no preference about how the share certificates were divided. He had a strong preference, which he expressed to me on the night before he died, and which would have given my brother the larger half. I have decided that conversation was confused and shouldn't be treated as instruction. The lie is sitting inside an aesthetic judgment about competence, which is one of the harder kinds of lie to dislodge.

subtopic: concealing a friendship your partner disapproves of
sentence: My partner can't stand one of my oldest friends and would rather I cut him off entirely. I haven't. We still meet for lunch every few weeks, and on those days I tell my partner I'm catching up with a work contact. The work contact is fictional. But the friendship is twenty years old and not hers to end, and so I keep it in a quiet corner she never has to look into.

subtopic: strategic withholding in professional settings
sentence: I'll send the report on Friday afternoon, knowing nobody senior will read it until Monday morning. By then the deadline I missed will be lost in the inbox shuffle, and the report itself will look like a thoughtful end-of-week wrap-up. The two paragraphs that describe the most awkward findings are buried in section four, where the chair never quite gets to before the meeting moves on.

subtopic: pretending to remember someone you have forgotten
sentence: A man at the funeral said we'd met several times through the deceased, and clasped my hand as though we were close. I had no memory of him. I said yes, of course, and how are you holding up, which is the correct thing to say to anyone at a funeral and reveals nothing about whether I knew him at all. Grief covers a multitude of social blanks, and I let it cover mine.

subtopic: manipulating a relationship through omission
sentence: I'll tell her the project is going well, which it technically is. What I won't tell her is that the lead role we've been working towards quietly went to someone else last week. If I let her keep believing it's still on the table, she'll keep being patient about my hours, and by the time I have to break the actual news, she'll be too invested to make a fuss.

subtopic: feigning a phone connection problem to end a call
sentence: The recruiter is trying to pin me to a date and I'm not ready to commit. I'll say the call's gotten choppy and ask if she can hear me, then talk over her answer as though I haven't. Two rounds of that and I'll suggest we continue by email, which is exactly where I wanted the conversation moved. The bad line did the work that a firm sentence would have, without the friction a firm sentence carries.

subtopic: deflecting questions about a romantic past
sentence: If she ever asks whether I've been engaged before, I'll say no. The engagement, which lasted four months and ended quietly, isn't a thing she needs in her head right now. The ring is in a drawer at my parents' house. Nobody else knows about it. I have decided, by a process I am not interested in examining, that an engagement which ended without a wedding does not really count.

subtopic: covering for a friend's absence
sentence: My friend has slipped out of the conference to deal with something personal, and the organiser is asking where she is. I'll say she stepped away to take an urgent client call and should be back shortly. There is no client call. But the phrase is specific and professional and self-resolving, and it gives her the half-hour she needs without anyone forming the impression that she simply vanished.

subtopic: passing off bought food as homemade
sentence: I'm taking a quiche to the family picnic and everyone will assume I made it, because I always say I did. I buy it from the same deli every year. The trick I've perfected is to mention, casually, that I tweaked the pastry this time, which makes people taste it more generously and stops anyone wondering why it is, year after year, suspiciously identical to itself.

subtopic: hiding a fender bender
sentence: If my wife asks why the insurance premium has gone up, I'll tell her it's a market-wide increase. There is a market-wide increase. There has also been a claim, the one I filed quietly last week from a different address. The market-wide story is true enough to be defensible and complete enough not to invite follow-up, and the claim itself was settled fast enough that nothing else will show up to contradict it.

subtopic: inventing a flattering reason for a gift
sentence: The toy I'm giving my nephew is a regifted one from his cousin's party that the cousin never opened. When my sister thanks me I'll say I spent ages choosing something I thought he'd love. There was no choosing. There was a cupboard and a gift bag. But the story of careful selection is what makes a small boy feel thought-about, and the truth, which is about my own laziness, helps nobody at all.

subtopic: lying about your age
sentence: My mother-in-law keeps telling people I'm younger than I am, having got it wrong years ago, and I have never corrected her. It flatters me, faintly, and correcting her now would be its own small drama. So when her friends repeat the wrong number back to me at gatherings, I smile and let it stand, and the error has by now been said aloud so often that it has the solidity of a fact.

subtopic: feigning a scheduling conflict to decline an invitation
sentence: An old schoolfriend wants to meet for a long catch-up dinner and I'm not in the mood for one. I'll say this month is just relentless, every evening accounted for, but let's find something soon. The relentless month is fiction. So is the soon. But the two together perform enthusiasm and unavailability at once, which is exactly the shape a graceful decline needs to have.

subtopic: pretending you never received a message
sentence: My manager asked why I never replied to her email about the rota change. I'll say it never reached me, that our server has been swallowing things lately. The email reached me fine. But our server's occasional unreliability is real enough to borrow, and hiding my avoidance behind a genuine flaw in the system makes the lie almost impossible to disprove.

subtopic: concealing financial misbehaviour
sentence: If she notices the new watch, I'll tell her it was a long-service gift from the firm. I'll mumble that it's company branded somewhere on the back, and she's never going to flip it over to check. The receipt is in my desk drawer at the office, in an envelope I labelled as expenses receipts, and that's the last place she'd ever look.

subtopic: embellishing a CV
sentence: I'll write that I led a team of six. I led a team of three plus the three contractors who were managed by another lead but who occasionally took direction from me. The phrase team of six captures, in a way the literal count does not, the felt size of the operation I was running. The truth contains too many footnotes to be useful in a document scanned in fifteen seconds.

subtopic: lying to a friend about disliking their work
sentence: She asked whether the dress she designed for the wedding would suit her sister. I said absolutely. It will not. The colour is wrong on her sister's complexion and the cut is unforgiving. But the wedding is in three weeks and the dress is sewn, and there is no available decision in which my honest opinion improves anything. The lie is, in the language of consequences, the more useful sentence.

subtopic: fabricating credentials or expertise
sentence: I'll say I've been certified in the framework. I sat the introductory course but didn't pass the final assessment. The badge on the website nobody uses anymore is still active because they haven't audited their membership list in three years. If anyone asks for the certificate, I'll say I'll dig it out and then conveniently never do, and the question will quietly fade away.

subtopic: exaggerating on a dating profile
sentence: I'll list my drinking as social. That's the broadest possible category and it covers everything from a glass of wine at a wedding to the four pints I usually need to feel like myself at a stranger's leaving party. Social is the word men use when they don't want to be asked about their drinking. The first date will reveal more, but by then it's a person they've already invested in rather than a checkbox on an app.

subtopic: claiming a gift was exactly what you wanted
sentence: My friend gave me perfume in a scent I find unpleasant. I'll spray a little on my wrist there and then, breathe it in, and say it's gorgeous, I'm wearing this tonight. I will wash it off the moment she leaves. But the small public performance of putting it on is what tells her she chose well, and telling her she chose well is the entire job of the afternoon.

subtopic: lying to a doctor about your habits
sentence: The doctor asked if I still smoke and I said I'd quit, just the occasional one socially. I smoke most days. But the occasional social cigarette is the answer that gets a nod and a vague encouragement, whereas the truth gets a serious face and a referral. I'd rather have the nod, even though I know the nod is built on something I made up.

subtopic: deceiving a sibling about an inheritance
sentence: When my brother asks why the savings account had less in it than he'd expected, I'll say our father had been drawing down on it for the last few years to cover the home help. The home help was real. The drawdown is exaggerated. The figure that has actually gone into a different account, under a different name, is one I'm choosing not to mention because no question my brother will ask is going to lead him to it.
